cases.title: Left Unilateral Neglect Following Right MCA Stroke — Inpatient Rehabilitation
cases.vignette: Mrs. Chen is a 68-year-old woman admitted to an inpatient rehabilitation unit five days ago following a right middle cerebral artery ischemic stroke. She presents with left hemiplegia, moderate left unilateral neglect, and mild dysphagia. She lives alone in a two-story home and expresses a strong desire to return there independently. Her daughter, who visits daily, reports concern about her mother's safety during self-care. The occupational therapist completed an initial evaluation using the Functional Independence Measure (FIM) and the Catherine Bergego Scale (CBS) to quantify neglect severity; the current FIM motor subscale score is 42 out of 91. During today's bathing session, Mrs. Chen consistently failed to wash her left arm and leg and did not apply deodorant to her left axilla. When the therapist drew her attention to the omissions, Mrs. Chen expressed genuine surprise, stating, 'I did not even realize I was missing that side.' The interprofessional team is meeting the following morning to discuss goals and discharge planning.

cases.title: Warehouse Worker with Lumbar Strain and Kinesiophobia in a Return-to-Work Program
cases.vignette: Marcus, a 42-year-old male warehouse worker, is referred to an occupational therapist through his employer's return-to-work (RTW) program following a lumbar strain sustained while lifting a 45 kg pallet 8 weeks ago. He completed acute physical therapy and has been cleared by his physician for light-duty work with restrictions: no lifting over 10 kg, limited bending and twisting, and maximum 4-hour workdays. Marcus reports pain rated 4/10 at rest and 7/10 with sustained bending. He expresses significant anxiety about re-injury and fears returning to full-duty tasks. Functional capacity evaluation (FCE) results indicate a safe lifting capacity of 8 kg with good body mechanics when verbally cued. Observation reveals habitual breath-holding, inconsistent lumbar protective strategies, and significant fear of movement, quantified by a Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia (TSK-17) score of 48 out of 68. Marcus's full job demands include repetitive lifting of 20–40 kg, prolonged standing, and pallet jack operation on the warehouse floor and an inclined loading dock. The OT has reviewed the job analysis report provided by the employer and completed a structured clinical interview.

cases.title: The Reluctant Resident: Parkinson's Disease and ADL Independence in Long-Term Care
cases.vignette: Margaret Chen is an 82-year-old woman admitted to a long-term care facility six weeks ago following a right total hip arthroplasty secondary to a fall-related femoral neck fracture. Her medical history includes Parkinson's disease (Hoehn & Yahr Stage III), mild cognitive impairment (MMSE 22/30), and osteoporosis. Prior to her fracture, she was fully independent in all activities of daily living and maintained an active lifestyle centered on knitting and gardening. Nursing staff report that she requires three to four minutes to initiate morning dressing, frequently freezes at the bathroom doorway, and becomes distressed when caregivers attempt to assist her, stating, "I can do it myself." She ambulates with a wheeled walker under supervision. Clinical observations reveal bilateral resting tremor (right greater than left), masked facies, hypophonia, and bradykinesia. Her daughter notes that symptoms are noticeably worse in the late afternoon, approximately one hour before her scheduled levodopa dose.

cases.title: Post-Stroke Rehabilitation of a Middle-Aged Professional With Left Hemiplegia and Hemispatial Neglect
cases.vignette:
Marcus is a 58-year-old right-handed high school principal admitted to an inpatient rehabilitation unit following a right middle cerebral artery (MCA) ischemic stroke 5 days ago. He presents with left hemiplegia, left hemispatial neglect, and mild executive dysfunction. Prior to admission, Marcus lived in a two-story home with his wife, managed all household finances, and coached youth basketball on weekends. His primary goal is to return home and eventually resume work.

On initial OT evaluation, Marcus scores 34/56 on the Functional Independence Measure (FIM). He requires moderate assistance for upper body dressing due to neglect-related errors — consistently omitting the left sleeve — and requires maximal assistance for lower body dressing and bathing. He is ambulatory with a quad cane and requires supervision on level surfaces but cannot safely navigate stairs. Cognitive screening reveals impaired sustained attention and difficulty with multi-step task sequencing. His wife is present and eager to participate in caregiver training. Discharge is planned in 14 days.

cases.title: Stroke Rehabilitation: Outcome-Driven Plan Revision and Fieldwork Mentorship
cases.vignette:
Mr. Delgado is a 68-year-old man admitted to an inpatient rehabilitation unit 12 days ago following a left hemisphere ischemic stroke. He presents with right hemiplegia, expressive aphasia, and moderate deficits in self-care performance. Prior to admission, he was independent in all activities of daily living and lived alone in a single-story home. He communicates preferences reliably through gestures and yes/no responses. His adult daughter attends therapy sessions when her work schedule permits.

Over the past week, the treating occupational therapist (OT) has been implementing a compensatory approach to upper-extremity dressing and grooming retraining. Upon reviewing Mr. Delgado's Functional Independence Measure (FIM) scores at the two-week mark, the OT identifies minimal functional gains. The OT recently reviewed a systematic review indicating that task-specific training combined with graded repetition produces superior upper-extremity outcomes compared to compensatory strategies alone for clients with moderate paresis at this stage of recovery. The rehabilitation unit has also recently welcomed a Level II fieldwork student, who will begin co-treating with the OT beginning next week.

cases.title: Left MCA Stroke with Right Hemiplegia and Neglect: Inpatient Rehabilitation
cases.vignette: Mr. Harold Chen, a 68-year-old retired chef, is admitted to an inpatient rehabilitation unit 5 days following a left middle cerebral artery (MCA) ischemic stroke. He presents with right-sided hemiplegia (upper extremity more involved than lower extremity), mild expressive aphasia with intact auditory comprehension, and right hemispatial neglect. Prior to the stroke, he was fully independent in all activities of daily living (ADLs) and instrumental ADLs (IADLs), including preparation of complex meals. He resides in a two-story home with his wife; the master bedroom and full bathroom are located on the second floor, and a half-bath is available on the ground floor. Mr. Chen expresses a strong desire to return home and resume cooking. Current functional status: he requires moderate assistance for upper body dressing, is dependent for lower body dressing, and requires verbal cueing for grooming tasks due to neglect. He is medically cleared for a regular diet with thin liquids. Cognitive screening reveals mild impairment in sustained attention and processing speed. He mobilizes within the unit via wheelchair with supervision.

cases.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis Flare: Community OT Intervention
cases.vignette: Margaret Chen is a 58-year-old bookkeeper who lives alone in a two-story home and attends the community health centre following a referral from her rheumatologist. She has a seven-year history of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and is currently experiencing a moderate disease flare. She reports bilateral hand pain rated 6/10 at rest, morning stiffness lasting approximately two and a half hours, and visible swelling across the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints of both hands. Margaret identifies three primary concerns: difficulty fastening buttons and managing zippers during morning dressing, inability to prepare her own meals due to impaired grip strength, and reduced speed and accuracy when typing at her computer for work. She works part-time from home three days per week and is anxious about her capacity to maintain employment. She reports that pain worsens significantly with sustained pinch grip. Grip strength measured with a dynamometer is 12 kg on the right and 9 kg on the left (normative mean for her age and sex is approximately 25 kg). She has no cognitive deficits and is highly motivated to regain independent function.

cases.title: Occupational Justice and Cultural Safety: A First Nations Elder in Long-Term Care
cases.vignette: Margaret is a 78-year-old Cree First Nations woman admitted three weeks ago to a long-term care facility following a right total hip arthroplasty after a fall at home. She lives far from her reserve community, and her closest family member — an adult daughter — visits only on weekends. Margaret speaks Cree as her primary language and has limited conversational English. Staff report that she rarely initiates communication, consistently declines group activities, and has significantly reduced her food intake. During the initial occupational therapy assessment, Margaret is withdrawn and does not make eye contact. When asked about her prior daily routines, she does not respond. The unit dietician has flagged her weight loss as a clinical concern. The care team attributes her withdrawal to post-operative depression. However, Margaret's daughter reports that her mother is grieving the loss of connection to her home community, land, and traditional practices — including morning prayer, beading, and preparing traditional foods. Her prayer items were placed in storage by staff upon admission, and the facility kitchen is accessible to staff only.

cases.title: Home Care OT Following Left MCA Stroke: Balancing Client-Centered Goals and Safe Participation
cases.vignette: Margaret Chen, a 74-year-old retired librarian, is seen by a home care OT three weeks after a left middle cerebral artery stroke resulting in mild right hemiplegia and expressive aphasia. She lives alone in a single-story home and was fully independent in all ADLs and IADLs prior to her stroke. During the initial visit, the OT observes Margaret struggling to fasten the buttons on her blouse during morning dressing. Margaret becomes visibly frustrated, repeatedly pointing to the buttons and using single words and gestures to communicate. Her daughter, who visits daily, reports that Margaret frequently refuses offered assistance and insists on attempting tasks independently. Environmental assessment of the bathroom reveals no grab bars, a standard bathtub with a high step-over threshold, and a loose bath mat on tile flooring. The OT notes Margaret demonstrates fair unsupported sitting balance, inconsistent standing balance, and uses her right hand minimally during bilateral tasks. Her home reflects an active prior life — books, hobby materials, and family photographs are visible throughout.

cases.title: Occupational Performance Decline in a Woman with Rheumatoid Arthritis
cases.vignette: Maria is a 58-year-old woman referred to the community health centre occupational therapist by her rheumatologist following a six-month history of worsening rheumatoid arthritis affecting her bilateral hands, wrists, and right knee. She works three days per week as an administrative assistant, performing extended keyboard use and filing. She lives alone in a second-floor apartment with no elevator. Maria reports two hours of morning stiffness, significant afternoon fatigue, and difficulty with meal preparation, dressing—particularly fastening bra hooks—and grocery shopping. She recently stopped knitting, a lifelong leisure pursuit, due to hand pain. A PHQ-9 completed at intake indicates mild depression with a score of 8. She reports feeling useless and fears losing her job. Physical examination reveals reduced grip strength bilaterally, active synovitis at the metacarpophalangeal joints, and mild right knee effusion. Her stated goals are to continue working and to resume knitting. The referring physician has cleared her for community-based occupational therapy.

cases.title: Navigating Cultural Safety and Self-Determination in Inpatient Stroke Rehabilitation
cases.vignette: Margaret is a 68-year-old First Nations woman from a remote northern community admitted to an urban inpatient rehabilitation unit following a left hemisphere ischemic stroke. She presents with moderate expressive aphasia, right upper extremity weakness, and dysphagia. Cree is her primary language; her English proficiency diminishes when she is fatigued or anxious. Her adult daughter, Rose, has traveled from their home community to be present at the hospital. Through Rose, Margaret has expressed significant distress at being separated from her land, community, and family. She practices daily smudging with sage, which holds deep spiritual importance; the unit has no formal policy regarding traditional healing practices. The rehabilitation team has scheduled Margaret for an initial ADL assessment at 8:00 AM, but Rose explains that mornings hold cultural and spiritual significance for Margaret and she strongly prefers not to be disturbed before mid-morning. The attending physician has asked the occupational therapist to complete assessments promptly given current length-of-stay targets.

cases.title: Resistive ADL Behavior in a Long-Term Care Resident with Moderate Alzheimer's Dementia
cases.vignette: Mrs. Eleanor Vasquez is an 82-year-old retired schoolteacher who has resided at Maplewood Long-Term Care Center for 14 months following a right total hip replacement secondary to a fracture. Her medical history includes moderate Alzheimer's dementia (MMSE 16/30), type 2 diabetes, and bilateral hand arthritis. Prior to admission she independently managed all personal ADLs, maintained a vegetable garden, and frequently read to her grandchildren. Nursing staff report that Mrs. Vasquez has become increasingly resistive during morning care, pushing staff away during bathing and dressing. Observation reveals she can follow one-step verbal directions and initiates familiar tasks but loses sequencing mid-task and cannot carry over two-step instructions. She demonstrates intact long-term memory, responds positively to 1960s music, and brightens when discussing her classroom or garden. She currently requires maximum assistance for lower-body dressing and moderate assistance for upper-body dressing. Hip precautions remain in effect. Her daughter, who visits weekly, requests information about how to support her mother's care and quality of life.

cases.title: Community OT with Margaret: Cultural Safety, Access, and Equity
cases.vignette: Margaret is a 58-year-old First Nations woman referred to a community health centre occupational therapist six weeks after a mild ischemic stroke. She lives alone in a ground-floor urban apartment; her two adult children visit on weekends. Since her stroke, Margaret reports difficulty with meal preparation, medication management, and community mobility. She uses a quad cane indoors and had relied on public transit prior to her stroke but has not returned to it since discharge. During the initial interview, Margaret shares that she attends a local Indigenous Friendship Centre weekly, values its cultural programming and social connection, and describes her community ties as central to her identity and well-being. She lives approximately 3 km from the health centre on a fixed income and has not yet received the home support services to which she was referred at hospital discharge. Margaret tells the OT that previous healthcare encounters have left her feeling dismissed and 'talked at,' and she expresses hesitation about whether this appointment will be any different.

cases.title: Early Parkinson's Disease: Occupational Performance Assessment at a Community Health Centre
cases.vignette: Margaret is a 68-year-old retired primary school teacher referred to the occupational therapist at a community health centre following a recent diagnosis of early-stage Parkinson's disease (Hoehn & Yahr Stage II). She lives alone in a single-story bungalow and drove herself to the appointment today. During the intake interview, Margaret reports increasing difficulty buttoning her blouse, writing cheques, and preparing her Sunday roast for visiting grandchildren. She describes these losses as "chipping away at who I am." Her husband passed away two years ago; family live three hours away and visit monthly. She receives no formal support services. Observation reveals bilateral resting tremor, mild bradykinesia, and subtle postural instability. A brief cognitive screen (MoCA) yields a score of 27/30. She is articulate, highly motivated, and expresses a clear desire to remain independent at home. The referring physician has asked OT to complete a functional assessment and recommend a management plan.

cases.title: Return to Occupation Following Major Depressive Disorder
cases.vignette: Maya is a 34-year-old woman referred to an outpatient occupational therapy clinic following a three-week partial hospitalization program for major depressive disorder (MDD). She lives alone in a second-floor apartment and has been on medical leave from her position as a graphic designer for four months. During the initial OT interview, Maya describes difficulty initiating morning self-care on most days, skipping meals because grocery shopping feels overwhelming, and complete disengagement from previously valued hobbies including drawing and photography. She reports little contact with friends or family and rates her afternoon energy level at 2 out of 10. Her psychiatrist stabilized her on a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor six weeks ago. Maya's primary goal is to return to part-time work within three months. Administration of the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM) yields a performance score of 3.2 out of 10 and a satisfaction score of 2.8 out of 10. Structured kitchen observation reveals intact motor skills but notably prolonged task initiation and reduced sequencing efficiency. No safety concerns are identified.

cases.title: Healing on Her Terms: Cultural Safety in Stroke Rehabilitation
cases.vignette: Margaret (Maggie) is a 58-year-old First Nations woman admitted to an inpatient rehabilitation unit following a left hemispheric stroke resulting in right-sided hemiparesis and mild expressive aphasia. She lives on a rural reserve approximately 300 km from the hospital. Since admission, Maggie has been accompanied by rotating family members who remain at bedside throughout the day and night. The treating team has observed that Maggie rarely makes eye contact during interprofessional assessments, provides brief verbal responses, and has declined two occupational therapy sessions this week. Nursing staff have documented concerns about "poor motivation" and "limited engagement with the rehabilitation program." Maggie's daughter explains that her mother is a knowledge keeper in their community and that healing, for their family, involves ceremony, community presence, and collective support. She formally requests that a local Elder be involved in her mother's care. The rehabilitation unit has a written policy affirming culturally safe care but no established protocol for Elder involvement. Maggie's stated discharge goal is to return home to her reserve, where she lives with extended family who have offered to provide daily physical assistance.

cases.title: Right MCA Stroke with Left Hemiplegia, Spatial Neglect, and Impaired Self-Awareness in Inpatient Rehab
cases.vignette: Marcus is a 58-year-old retired high school teacher admitted to an inpatient rehabilitation unit 5 days after a right middle cerebral artery (MCA) ischemic stroke. He lives alone in a two-story home and identifies meal preparation and driving as his highest-priority occupations. Chart review reveals left hemiplegia (shoulder flexion 2/5, hand grip 1/5) with intact right upper extremity function. Left unilateral spatial neglect is confirmed by the Star Cancellation Test, on which Marcus missed 9 of 13 left-sided targets. The Mini-Mental State Examination score is 24/30, with errors on orientation and short-term recall. Marcus ambulates 20 feet with a rolling walker and maximum assistance due to left-sided weakness and impulsive safety behaviors, including initiating transfers without notifying staff. He expresses high motivation to return home within two weeks, which is shorter than the team's projected 3- to 4-week stay. When asked about his deficits, Marcus denies difficulty with any task and attributes his slow movement to being out of practice.

cases.title: Post-Stroke Discharge Planning in Acute Care: Right MCA Stroke with Left Neglect and Anosognosia
cases.vignette: Marcus Chen, a 68-year-old retired engineer, is admitted to an acute care hospital ward following a right middle cerebral artery (MCA) ischemic stroke three days ago. He presents with left-sided hemiplegia (upper extremity strength 1/5, lower extremity 2+/5), left hemispatial neglect, and anosognosia — he insists he is "perfectly fine" and ready to go home. His medical history includes type 2 diabetes and hypertension. Prior to admission, Marcus lived alone in a two-story home, was fully independent in all ADLs and IADLs, drove independently, and was an avid woodworker. During the bedside OT assessment, Marcus is alert and communicates in complete sentences but demonstrates impulsivity and poor safety awareness during mobility tasks. He requires maximum assistance for upper body dressing and consistently fails to attend to stimuli on his left side, including food on the left half of his meal tray. His daughter, who lives 30 minutes away, works full-time and can provide evening support only. The medical team is targeting discharge within 48 to 72 hours.

cases.title: Post-Stroke Acute Care: Left MCA Infarct with Aphasia and Right Hemiplegia
cases.vignette: Mrs. Chen is a 68-year-old right-handed retired teacher admitted to the acute care ward on post-stroke day 2 following a left middle cerebral artery (MCA) ischemic stroke. She presents with moderate right-sided hemiplegia, Broca's aphasia (severely limited verbal output with relatively preserved auditory comprehension), and mild left hemispatial neglect. Medical history includes type 2 diabetes and hypertension, both well-controlled prior to admission. She lives with her adult daughter in a two-story home and was independent in all activities of daily living (ADLs) and instrumental ADLs before this event. Nursing staff document difficulty during morning care routines, noting patient distress and inconsistent cooperation. The patient's right upper extremity is flaccid. Her daughter is present at the bedside and reports that Mrs. Chen becomes visibly frustrated when unable to communicate her needs. She was an avid cook and reader before the stroke. Medical status is stable and the team has placed an occupational therapy consult for evaluation and intervention.

cases.title: Motor Coordination Difficulties in a Third-Grade Boy Referred to School OT
cases.vignette: Marcus is an 8-year-old third-grade boy referred to the school-based occupational therapist by his classroom teacher. His teacher reports that Marcus takes twice as long as peers to complete written assignments, erases so forcefully that he frequently tears the paper, and produces illegible handwriting despite repeated direct instruction. In the cafeteria, Marcus avoids the self-serve station, struggles to manage utensils, and often eats with his fingers instead. He requires adult assistance each morning to button his school uniform and cannot independently tie his shoes. During recess, Marcus avoids the climbing structures and monkey bars, preferring sedentary bench activities. School records indicate no diagnosed medical conditions, normal vision and hearing screenings, and average intellectual ability confirmed by recent psychologist testing. Classroom accommodations including a pencil grip and a slant board have been trialed without measurable improvement. Marcus's parents corroborate the school's observations and describe significant morning-routine frustration at home. No behavioral concerns or sensory-seeking behaviors are noted in the referral.

cases.title: Caught Between Systems: First Nations Warehouse Supervisor in a Graduated Return-to-Work Program
cases.vignette: Marcus is a 38-year-old First Nations man employed as a warehouse supervisor at a large regional distribution company. He sustained a rotator cuff injury six months ago and has been on workers' compensation leave. An occupational therapist has been coordinating a graduated return-to-work (GRTW) plan on behalf of the insurer. During intake, Marcus discloses that previous healthcare providers attributed his slow recovery to lifestyle choices, leaving him reluctant to trust the process. He lives two hours from the nearest rehabilitation clinic and relies entirely on public transit. Marcus shares that collective decision-making — involving his adult daughter and a community Elder — is central to how he approaches significant life decisions, including his health care. His employer has been pressing the OT for a faster return timeline, citing operational demands. Standardized functional capacity assessments place Marcus within the modified-duties threshold, yet he reports persistent fatigue and pain he feels have not been taken seriously. He scores within limits on all administered measures but states, 'The numbers don't tell the whole story.'

cases.title: Return to Home After Left Hemisphere Ischemic Stroke
cases.vignette:
Marta Chen, a 68-year-old retired schoolteacher, is admitted to an inpatient rehabilitation unit 5 days after sustaining a left hemisphere ischemic stroke. She presents with right-sided hemiplegia, trace active movement at the right shoulder only, and mild expressive aphasia; receptive communication and cognition are intact. Prior to her stroke, Marta lived alone in a two-story home and was fully independent in all ADLs and IADLs, drove independently, and regularly prepared meals for her family on weekends. She expresses a strong desire to return home and resume these roles.

On the unit, Marta requires moderate assistance for upper-body dressing due to right upper extremity (UE) involvement and early fatigue. She transfers from bed to wheelchair with stand-by assistance using her left side. She becomes visibly frustrated when attempting to button her blouse. A kitchen assessment conducted later in the admission reveals she can safely operate the stovetop with her left hand but cannot open jars, carry filled pots, or use a standard can opener. The rehabilitation team has an anticipated 14-day inpatient stay before reassessment for discharge planning. The OT is initiating a comprehensive evaluation to establish client-centered goals.

cases.title: Marcus — Sensory Processing and Handwriting in Second Grade
cases.vignette: Marcus is a 7-year-old boy in second grade referred to the school-based occupational therapist by his classroom teacher due to illegible handwriting, frequent out-of-seat behavior, and refusal to participate in art activities. His mother reports he avoids certain clothing textures, has significant food-texture aversions, and frequently bumps into furniture and peers. During classroom observation, Marcus chews on his pencil, covers his ears during activity transitions, and persistently seeks physical movement. He holds his pencil with a rigid, tight grasp and produces poorly formed letters despite demonstrating adequate hand strength on informal assessment. Standardized testing using the Sensory Processing Measure, Second Edition (SPM-2) reveals elevated scores in the tactile, proprioceptive, and visual processing domains. The Bruininks-Oseretsky Test of Motor Proficiency, Second Edition (BOT-2) places his fine motor precision at the 12th percentile. His teacher notes he performs best during structured, predictable routines and struggles significantly during unstructured transitions between activities.

cases.title: Rotator Cuff Injury — Graduated Return to Work for a Registered Nurse
cases.vignette: Maria is a 42-year-old registered nurse employed full-time on a medical-surgical unit at a regional hospital. Eight weeks ago, she sustained a right rotator cuff partial-thickness tear during a patient repositioning task and was placed on modified duty. Her orthopedic surgeon has cleared her for a graduated return-to-work (RTW) program with the following restrictions: no lifting greater than 5 lbs above shoulder height and no repetitive overhead reaching. Maria reports right shoulder pain rated 4/10 at rest and 7/10 during overhead activities. She scores 32/40 on the Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia, indicating elevated fear of movement and re-injury. She is motivated to return to full duties but expresses significant anxiety about performing patient transfers. Her employer has formally requested she return to full nursing duties within 4 weeks. Maria's job demands include patient repositioning, overhead supply retrieval, medication administration, and electronic documentation. An occupational therapist has been referred to coordinate the RTW program and conduct an initial evaluation.

cases.title: Post-Operative Hip Fracture in an Older Adult with Mild Cognitive Impairment
cases.vignette: Mabel Chen is a 74-year-old woman admitted to the acute care ward following a mechanical fall at home that resulted in a left femoral neck fracture. She underwent open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) via a posterior approach and is currently on post-operative day 2. Her medical history includes mild cognitive impairment (MCI), type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypertension. She resides alone in a two-story home and reports she was previously independent in all activities of daily living (ADLs) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs). Posterior hip precautions are in effect: no hip flexion beyond 90 degrees, no internal rotation, and no adduction past midline. She is partial weight-bearing on the left lower extremity per surgeon orders. On the OT's initial visit, Mabel is alert and oriented to person and place but not to date. She becomes visibly anxious when asked to perform tasks and states, 'I just want to go back to my own home.' Nursing administered the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) on admission; Mabel scored 19 out of 30.

cases.title: Return to Routine Following Psychiatric Hospitalization for Major Depressive Disorder
cases.vignette: Maria is a 38-year-old graphic designer referred to outpatient occupational therapy four weeks after discharge from a 10-day psychiatric hospitalization for major depressive disorder (MDD). She lives alone in a second-floor apartment and has been on medical leave for three months. Her psychiatrist reports she has been medically stable on antidepressants for six weeks. During the initial OT evaluation, Maria states her primary goal is to return to work. She reports taking up to three hours to get out of bed each morning, frequently skipping meals, and not showering consistently over the past two weeks. She endorses significant fatigue, low motivation, and difficulty sustaining concentration beyond 20 minutes. Maria has stopped painting and hiking, two leisure activities she previously valued highly. The Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM) yields a performance score of 3.5 out of 10 and a satisfaction score of 2 out of 10 across self-care, productivity, and leisure domains. Maria becomes tearful when discussing her inability to manage basic daily tasks, stating, 'I used to be so organized.'

cases.title: Post-Stroke Occupational Rehabilitation in a Community Health Centre
cases.vignette: Maria is a 55-year-old right-handed elementary school teacher referred to the community health centre occupational therapist three months after sustaining a left middle cerebral artery ischemic stroke. She presents with mild right upper extremity weakness (grip strength 3+/5), moderate post-stroke fatigue rated 7/10 on the Fatigue Severity Scale, and mild expressive aphasia. Maria lives alone in a two-story townhome and has recently returned to part-time teaching three days per week. During the initial interview, she becomes tearful when describing difficulty buttoning her work blouses and chopping vegetables during meal preparation. She also expresses a strong desire to resume knitting, a daily hobby she practiced for 30 years. Maria's adult children live in another city, and she manages her home independently. She is medically stable and takes antihypertensives and a statin. Her physician has cleared her for outpatient rehabilitation. She identifies resuming full-time teaching, managing meal preparation independently, and returning to knitting as her three priority goals.

cases.title: Cultural Safety and Advocacy in Acute Stroke Rehabilitation for a First Nations Patient
cases.vignette: Aroha, a 58-year-old First Nations woman from a remote northern community, is admitted to an acute care hospital ward following a right-sided stroke resulting in left-sided weakness and mild expressive communication difficulties. She speaks English as a second language and primarily communicates in her Indigenous language with family members who have traveled over six hours to be present. The acute care team has requested an occupational therapy (OT) assessment for activities of daily living (ADL) and discharge planning. During the initial introduction, Aroha avoids eye contact, gives minimal verbal responses, and declines to attempt the standardized functional assessment. Her adult daughter explains that Aroha is uncomfortable with the hospital environment and that important decisions are made collectively by family in their community. The ward nurse notes there is pressure to discharge Aroha within 48 hours due to bed availability. The OT also learns that the discharge destination — Aroha's remote community — has no local allied health follow-up services, and that a culturally specific inpatient rehabilitation program exists 400 km away but has not yet been mentioned to Aroha or her family.

cases.title: Post-Stroke Rehabilitation: Right Hemiplegia and Expressive Aphasia
cases.vignette: Mr. Gerald Okafor is a 65-year-old right-handed retired contractor admitted to an inpatient rehabilitation unit 10 days after a left hemisphere ischemic stroke. He lives with his wife in a single-story home with three entry steps. Prior to his stroke he was independent in all activities of daily living (ADLs) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs), drove independently, and volunteered weekly at his church. His current presentation includes right-sided hemiplegia with proximal right upper extremity (RUE) strength at 3/5 and distal strength at 1/5, consistent with Brunnstrom Stage III recovery. Bilateral sensation is intact. He presents with mild-to-moderate expressive aphasia with preserved receptive language and mild executive dysfunction noted on chart review. He becomes visibly frustrated during therapy sessions. Functional Independence Measure (FIM) scores on admission indicate moderate assistance required for upper body dressing, grooming, and bathing. His wife reports he was fiercely independent and is requesting full caregiver training for all ADLs. Mr. Okafor himself communicates through gestures and yes/no responses that he strongly wants to regain use of his right hand. Projected discharge is in nine days.

cases.title: Home Care OT: Urban First Nations Woman Post-Stroke
cases.vignette: Marie is a 72-year-old First Nations woman living alone in a subsidized urban apartment. She was referred to home care occupational therapy eight weeks after a mild ischemic stroke that left her with mild left upper extremity weakness and persistent fatigue. On the first visit, the OT observes the apartment is sparsely furnished and the kitchen has very limited food supplies. Marie is quiet during the initial interview, offering brief responses. When asked about her daily routine, she describes spending mornings doing beadwork, calling it 'important work that keeps me connected.' She declines the OT's suggestion to trial adaptive equipment for beadwork, saying she would rather find her own way. Marie mentions she occasionally skips meals when her energy is low. She states clearly that she wants to remain in her own home. The OT learns that Marie's daughter, who lives two hours away, has already contacted the referring physician requesting a long-term care placement, citing concerns about her mother's nutrition and safety.

cases.title: Navigating Cultural Safety and Equity in Elementary School OT Practice
cases.vignette: Marcus is an 8-year-old First Nations boy referred to the school-based occupational therapist (OT) by his Grade 3 teacher for concerns about handwriting legibility and difficulty completing pencil-and-paper tasks. Marcus lives with his grandmother, Ellen, who is his primary caregiver and speaks English as a second language. Ellen has expressed hesitation about formal assessment, stating that previous school professionals have labeled Marcus without consulting the family. She notes that Marcus demonstrates strong spatial reasoning and practical skills in traditional activities at home. The OT observes that the classroom environment relies primarily on Western academic formats, and Marcus appears withdrawn during structured seat-based tasks but highly engaged during hands-on activities. The school psychologist has recommended a standardized battery, and the principal is pressing for documentation to justify resource allocation. The OT must balance institutional demands, the family's lived experience of systemic marginalization within educational systems, and Marcus's occupational performance needs across contexts.

cases.title: Home Care OT Following Posterior Total Hip Arthroplasty
cases.vignette: Margaret Chen is a 72-year-old retired teacher referred for home occupational therapy services 3 weeks following a right total hip arthroplasty via posterior approach. She lives alone in a single-story ranch home with two entry steps and no grab bars. Her adult daughter visits on weekends only. On the initial home visit, the occupational therapist observes Margaret ambulating with a front-wheeled walker but notes significant trunk forward-flexion when rising from her standard-height chair and during toilet transfers. Margaret reports pain of 4/10 with activity. Her stated priorities are returning to independent grocery shopping and gardening. She was discharged from the hospital with a reacher, long-handled sponge, and sock aid but reports ongoing difficulty with lower-body dressing despite using these devices. Her bathroom has a step-in tub and shower combination. Cognitive screening is intact. Margaret is highly motivated but expresses frustration, stating she feels helpless. She has declined a raised toilet seat, saying adaptive equipment makes her feel like an invalid.

cases.title: Post-Surgical Recovery and Cultural Safety at a Community Health Centre
cases.vignette: Maria is a 58-year-old First Nations woman referred to the community health centre occupational therapist following a right total hip replacement performed six weeks ago. She recently relocated from her home reserve to stay with her adult daughter in the city during recovery. The referral note from the surgeon describes Maria as 'non-compliant with physiotherapy' and 'resistant to discharge planning.' During the initial OT session, Maria speaks quietly, avoids sustained eye contact, and responds to questions with brief answers. When asked about her rehabilitation goals, she says, 'Whatever you think is best — you're the expert.' She then mentions, almost in passing, that she hopes to return home to her reserve to care for her two grandchildren and attend seasonal community ceremonies, but adds, 'I suppose that's not realistic with this hip.' A review of her chart reveals that all prior appointments were scheduled without consulting her availability, and no transportation support was arranged despite a documented lack of access to a vehicle. There is no record of a culturally adapted functional assessment or of any discussion of her home and community environment.

cases.title: Mrs. Chen: Parkinson's Disease, Total Hip Replacement, and Discharge Planning in Long-Term Care
cases.vignette: Mrs. Eleanor Chen is a 78-year-old woman residing in a long-term care facility following a right total hip replacement via posterior surgical approach six weeks ago. She has pre-existing moderate Parkinson's disease (Hoehn & Yahr Stage III) and mild neurocognitive disorder (MoCA score 21/30, with deficits in executive function and short-term memory). Prior to admission, Mrs. Chen lived alone in a second-floor apartment and was independent in all activities of daily living. She currently presents with bilateral resting tremors (left greater than right), bradykinesia, intermittent freezing episodes during movement initiation, and masked facial expression. She requires moderate assistance for bathing and upper and lower body dressing, and is on fall precautions secondary to orthostatic hypotension. Levodopa-carbidopa is administered at 7:00 a.m. and 1:00 p.m. Her apartment has three exterior stairs with no railing and a small bathroom with no grab bars. Mrs. Chen's primary stated goal is to return home. Her adult son believes she should transition to an assisted living facility, citing safety concerns. The occupational therapist has initiated a comprehensive ADL evaluation and discharge planning process.

cases.title: Maria: Reconnecting with Meaning in Mental Health Outpatient Care
cases.vignette: Maria is a 38-year-old First Nations woman referred to a mental health outpatient clinic for persistent depression and anxiety following a significant family loss. She lives 45 minutes from the clinic by bus, has two young children, and is currently staying in transitional housing after losing her apartment. Maria completed intake paperwork in English, although she mentioned that her first language is Cree and she sometimes struggles to find precise words when discussing emotional experiences. During the initial OT session, she speaks briefly and makes limited eye contact while responding to standardized assessment questions. She discloses that she has had negative experiences with social services in the past and is uncertain whether she can trust the current healthcare team. She expresses a strong interest in reconnecting with beadwork and spending time on the land — activities that held deep meaning before her circumstances became difficult. A community Elder has offered to support her recovery but has not yet been formally incorporated into her care. The OT is now planning the occupational profile and collaborative goal-setting process.

cases.title: Marcus: Handwriting and Sensory Processing Challenges in Third Grade
cases.vignette: Marcus is an 8-year-old, third-grade student referred to school-based OT by his classroom teacher due to illegible handwriting, difficulty completing written assignments within allotted time, and frequent avoidance of tabletop tasks. His teacher reports he often leaves his seat, fidgets with school supplies, and becomes visibly distressed during art and craft activities. Marcus's parents note he has always been "clumsy" and resists wearing certain clothing textures. Classroom observation reveals Marcus grips his pencil with excessive force, erases frequently, and produces letters inconsistent in size and spacing. Standardized assessment using the Bruininks-Oseretsky Test of Motor Proficiency, Second Edition (BOT-2) yields scores in the at-risk range for fine motor precision and fine motor integration. The Sensory Profile 2 — School Companion identifies elevated tactile sensitivity and low registration in proprioception. Marcus is verbal and academically capable, expressing frustration by telling his teacher, "My hand just won't do what my brain says." He currently participates in general education with no formal accommodations in place.

cases.title: Home-Based OT for a Client with Moderate Parkinson's Disease
cases.vignette: Mr. G is a 68-year-old retired teacher with moderate Parkinson's disease (Hoehn & Yahr Stage III) referred for home-based occupational therapy. He lives with his wife, Margaret, in a single-story home. During the initial home visit, the OT observes bilateral resting tremor, mild cogwheel rigidity in both upper extremities, and intermittent freezing of gait when passing through narrow doorways. Mr. G reports significant difficulty initiating morning dressing tasks and completing his shower routine safely; he frequently skips breakfast because cutting food has become too frustrating. Margaret assists him with most ADLs but describes feeling exhausted and overwhelmed. On observation, Mr. G requires moderate assistance for lower-body dressing and minimal assistance for upper-body tasks. He scores 18/30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), indicating mild cognitive impairment. His oral levodopa is taken at 7:00 AM, with peak motor benefit typically occurring 60 to 90 minutes later. Mr. G's stated priority is to become more independent in his morning routine so that Margaret can rest.

cases.title: The Reluctant Return: Occupational Reintegration in Major Depressive Disorder
cases.vignette: Maya Chen, a 34-year-old graphic designer, is referred to occupational therapy at a community mental health outpatient clinic following a diagnosis of major depressive disorder (MDD) four months ago. She lives alone in an apartment. Over the past four months she has withdrawn from her weekly pottery class, rarely leaves home except for medical appointments, and has missed multiple work deadlines due to difficulty initiating tasks and concentrating. She describes her mornings as 'impossible,' reporting she spends two to three hours in bed before rising, skips meals regularly, and wears the same clothing for days at a time. Her psychiatrist stabilized her on an antidepressant six weeks ago, and she reports mild mood improvement but states, 'I just cannot seem to get myself going.' Maya identifies returning to full-time graphic design work and resuming pottery as her top priorities. Her self-care, meal preparation, productivity, and leisure participation are all significantly impaired. Insight is intact; she denies active suicidal ideation. Affect is constricted but Maya engages cooperatively with the OT.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with idiopathic Parkinson's disease (Hoehn & Yahr Stage III) is referred to OT following two near-fall incidents during morning dressing. He takes levodopa/carbidopa and his wife reports predictable ON/OFF motor fluctuations throughout the day. Dressing takes approximately 90 minutes; the wife waits nearby "in case." The client states that dressing independently is his top priority and that his wife's presence makes him feel like "an invalid." Evaluation reveals significant bradykinesia, episodic freezing when navigating the narrow doorway between the bedroom and bathroom, mild visuospatial difficulty, and fully intact cognition. He performs sit-to-stand from a standard chair with mild effort but no loss of balance. Which intervention plan BEST addresses this client's occupational performance priorities and aligns with current evidence for Parkinson's disease?
questions.correct_rationale: Option A integrates three pillars of evidence-based OT practice for Parkinson's disease: (1) Activity scheduling during peak ON periods leverages the predictable pharmacokinetic window of levodopa/carbidopa, maximizing motor availability for a demanding ADL. (2) Long-handled devices and a button hook reduce the fine-motor and postural demands of dressing without eliminating the client's active role, directly preserving independence — his stated priority. (3) Rhythmic auditory cueing (e.g., counting, metronome beats) is supported by robust evidence for reducing freezing of gait in PD by engaging intact subcortical timing pathways when basal ganglia output is impaired. Together these strategies address the client's occupational performance deficits with compensatory techniques that match the progressive nature of the condition, respect his autonomy, and are actionable without waiting for medical changes.
questions.core_concept: In progressive neurological conditions with fluctuating motor performance, evidence-based OT selects time-contingent compensation (scheduling to ON periods), task modification (adaptive equipment), and neurorehabilitation cueing strategies (auditory/visual rhythmic cues for freezing) rather than remediation alone or caregiver substitution. This reflects the occupational therapy principle of matching intervention approach to the nature of the condition, performance context, and client's valued roles — not defaulting to the safest or most restrictive option.
questions.explain_differently: Think of it like this: the client's motor system is not broken all day — it has reliable windows of better function tied to his medication. A skilled OT acts like a coach who schedules practice during the best conditions, gives the athlete better tools (adaptive equipment), and teaches a trick (rhythmic cueing) to break through a specific stuck point (doorway freezing). Option A does all three things at once, while the other options either take the game away from the athlete entirely (B), only work on fitness without addressing the specific game situation (C), or tell the athlete to wait in the locker room until the coach is ready (D).
questions.topic: Parkinson's Disease — ADL Intervention, Compensatory Strategies, and Activity Scheduling

options.label: A
options.text: Schedule dressing tasks to occur during the client's peak ON period, introduce long-handled adaptive equipment and a button hook, and train the client in rhythmic auditory cueing strategies to manage freezing episodes during doorway navigation.

options.label: B
options.text: Train the wife in hands-on physical assistance techniques for all morning dressing tasks, and prescribe a shower chair and tub transfer bench to reduce energy expenditure and eliminate fall risk.
options.incorrect_rationale: This approach addresses safety by substituting caregiver assistance for the client's independence, directly contradicting his highest-priority occupational goal and violating client-centered practice without clinical justification for full dependence at this stage.

options.label: C
options.text: Implement a progressive resistance exercise program targeting trunk and lower-extremity musculature to remediate bradykinesia and improve postural stability during dressing.
options.incorrect_rationale: While exercise has a role in PD management, a purely restorative approach does not address the fluctuating, time-dependent nature of ON/OFF motor performance or the freezing episodes, and it fails to offer the client functional gains in the near term.

options.label: D
options.text: Defer active OT intervention and refer back to the neurologist to optimize levodopa timing first, explaining to the client that meaningful functional progress requires stable medication management.
options.incorrect_rationale: OT intervention is indicated concurrently with medical management, not sequentially; identifying and scheduling tasks around ON periods is itself a core OT competency, and deferral unnecessarily delays client-centered care.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is beginning a new therapeutic relationship with an Indigenous client. Which of the following actions BEST reflects the principle of cultural safety?
questions.correct_rationale: Cultural safety is defined by the recipient of care, not by the provider. By directly asking the client how they prefer to engage and what feels respectful, the therapist transfers power to the client, honors self-determination, and creates the conditions under which the client — not the clinician — decides whether the interaction is safe. This aligns with core anti-oppressive and client-centred practice.
questions.core_concept: Cultural safety is a framework in which the client, not the clinician, determines whether an interaction feels safe, respectful, and free from discrimination. It requires practitioners to reflect on their own power, assumptions, and potential biases, and to create relational conditions where clients can participate as their full selves without risk of cultural harm.
questions.explain_differently: Think of it this way: cultural safety is not something the therapist can decide they have provided — it is something the client experiences. Just as you cannot declare a ramp "accessible" without asking the wheelchair user whether it actually works for them, you cannot declare care "culturally safe" without asking the client. Handing the steering wheel to the client by asking about their preferences is what makes the difference.
questions.topic: Cultural Safety and Indigenous Client-Centred Practice

options.label: A
options.text: Complete a cultural competence training module before the first session to ensure preparedness.
options.incorrect_rationale: Completing a training module builds awareness but does not itself create cultural safety, which is relational and must be co-created with the individual client rather than established in advance through education alone.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask the client how they prefer to engage and what feels respectful within their care.

options.label: C
options.text: Incorporate traditional healing practices from the client's nation into the treatment plan.
options.incorrect_rationale: Assuming the client wants traditional healing without asking first is presumptuous and risks stereotyping; not all Indigenous clients identify with or wish to integrate traditional practices, and this decision belongs to the client.

options.label: D
options.text: Ensure the clinic environment displays culturally relevant artwork and imagery.
options.incorrect_rationale: Culturally inclusive physical spaces are a positive step but are insufficient on their own; cultural safety is relational and experiential, not achieved through environmental decoration alone.

questions.stem: A newly licensed occupational therapist seeks guidance from a seasoned OT colleague who agrees to meet regularly, share professional wisdom, help shape the new therapist's career goals, and provide ongoing encouragement through workplace challenges. This professional relationship is BEST described as:
questions.correct_rationale: Mentorship is a voluntary, longitudinal relationship in which an experienced professional (the mentor) intentionally supports a less experienced colleague's overall professional growth — sharing knowledge, modeling professional identity, assisting with goal-setting, and providing psychosocial support. All elements in the stem (ongoing meetings, career guidance, knowledge sharing, encouragement) align precisely with the defining features of mentorship as described in AOTA's professional engagement literature.
questions.core_concept: Mentorship is one of several key forms of professional engagement in occupational therapy. It is distinguished from supervision, consultation, and education by its voluntary, relationship-centered, long-term focus on the mentee's holistic professional development rather than on evaluating competence or solving a discrete clinical problem.
questions.explain_differently: Think of mentorship like an experienced guide walking alongside a new hiker on an unfamiliar trail — the guide isn't grading the hiker's every step (that would be supervision) or just answering one quick question about the map (that would be consultation). The guide is invested in the whole journey, sharing hard-won wisdom, helping chart the route ahead, and cheering the hiker on. That sustained, growth-oriented companionship is the defining feature of mentorship.
questions.topic: Professional Engagement in Occupational Therapy — Mentorship

options.label: A
options.text: Clinical supervision
options.incorrect_rationale: Clinical supervision is a formal, often legally required oversight relationship focused on evaluating client care competence and protecting the public, not primarily on long-term career development.

options.label: B
options.text: Peer consultation
options.incorrect_rationale: Peer consultation is a lateral, task-specific exchange between colleagues of similar experience level to problem-solve a particular clinical situation, not an ongoing developmental relationship between an experienced and novice professional.

options.label: C
options.text: Mentorship
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer; mentorship is a voluntary, longitudinal relationship in which an experienced professional supports a less experienced colleague's overall professional growth through knowledge sharing, goal-setting, and psychosocial support.

options.label: D
options.text: Professional in-service training
options.incorrect_rationale: In-service training is a structured, typically employer-organized educational session targeting a specific skill or policy update, not a sustained one-on-one developmental relationship.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist conducts an initial assessment with a 35-year-old Somali-Canadian woman referred for community mental health services due to depression. When asked to complete a standardized self-report questionnaire, the client declines, explaining that disclosing personal struggles to someone she does not yet know conflicts with her family's values. Which action BEST demonstrates culturally safe, client-centred practice?
questions.correct_rationale: Option B enacts cultural humility and client-centred practice simultaneously. By inviting the client to define what she is comfortable sharing and co-designing the assessment approach, the OT treats her values as clinically relevant rather than as a compliance obstacle. Standardized tools are instruments that serve assessment goals, not prerequisites that override those goals; adapting methodology to the client's cultural context while still gathering occupationally relevant information is a core CAOT and WFOT competency. This approach also preserves the therapeutic alliance at a moment that is often formative for clients from communities with historical reasons to distrust health institutions.
questions.core_concept: Cultural safety requires practitioners to critically examine how institutionalized assessment practices — including mandated standardized tools — can reproduce power imbalances and exclude clients whose worldviews do not align with Western biomedical frameworks. The competency is not cultural knowledge about a specific group, but the reflexive willingness to adapt methodology collaboratively rather than requiring the client to conform to the dominant system.
questions.explain_differently: The questionnaire is a road, not the destination. The destination is understanding this person's occupational life well enough to help her. If the road she has been handed is blocked by a legitimate cultural boundary, a skilled OT does not insist she walk it anyway, nor does the OT give up and go home — the OT says, "Okay, let's find a path together." That collaborative re-routing, with the client navigating, is exactly what culturally safe practice looks like in the room.
questions.topic: Cultural safety and adaptation of assessment practice for clients from diverse cultural backgrounds

options.label: A
options.text: Explain that the questionnaire is a required component of the agency's intake protocol and offer to complete it together in a supportive, step-by-step manner.
options.incorrect_rationale: Prioritizing agency protocol over the client's expressed cultural values signals that institutional compliance matters more than the therapeutic relationship, undermining cultural safety from the outset.

options.label: B
options.text: Arrange for a colleague who shares a similar cultural background to co-facilitate the session to help bridge the cultural gap.
options.incorrect_rationale: Assuming shared heritage will resolve the client's concern stereotypes her individual experience, bypasses her own voice in problem-solving, and does not address the relational trust that is the actual underlying barrier.

options.label: C
options.text: Defer the formal assessment and schedule a follow-up appointment after the client has had time to build rapport with the therapist naturally.
options.incorrect_rationale: Passive deferral without a collaborative plan avoids rather than addresses the issue, delays meaningful engagement, and is not a proactive adaptation of practice to meet the client's needs.

options.label: D
options.text: Invite the client to share what she is comfortable discussing, and collaboratively identify assessment approaches that align with her values and occupational priorities.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer and does not have an incorrect rationale.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist working in a memory care setting is choosing an intervention for a client recently diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment. She reviews two recent systematic reviews on cognitive rehabilitation strategies, reflects on her three years of experience treating similar clients, and spends time asking the client which daily activities he most wants to be able to continue performing independently. Which component of evidence-based practice (EBP) does asking the client about his activity priorities represent?
questions.correct_rationale: Evidence-based practice in occupational therapy integrates three equally essential pillars: best available research evidence, the practitioner's clinical expertise, and the client's values, preferences, and goals. Asking the client which occupations he most wants to preserve directly captures his personal priorities — the third pillar. Ignoring this component and relying solely on research or clinical experience would violate client-centered EBP principles.
questions.core_concept: Evidence-based practice (EBP) in occupational therapy is built on three interdependent pillars: (1) best available external research evidence, (2) the clinician's expertise and professional judgment, and (3) the client's values, preferences, and goals. All three must be integrated for practice to be truly evidence-based and client-centered.
questions.explain_differently: Think of EBP as a three-legged stool: research, therapist expertise, and the client's own voice. If you take away the client's leg — his goals and what matters to him — the stool falls over. Asking the client what he wants to keep doing in daily life is exactly that third leg. No matter how strong the research or how skilled the therapist, a plan built without the client's priorities is not evidence-based by definition.
questions.topic: Evidence-Based Practice — Three Pillars (Client Values and Preferences)

options.label: A
options.text: Client values, preferences, and goals

options.label: B
options.text: Best available external research evidence
options.incorrect_rationale: External research evidence refers to findings from systematic reviews, RCTs, and peer-reviewed studies — not to information gathered directly from the client about personal priorities.

options.label: C
options.text: Clinical expertise and professional reasoning
options.incorrect_rationale: Clinical expertise reflects the practitioner's accumulated knowledge and judgment from experience, not the client's own expressed preferences or goals.

options.label: D
options.text: Outcome measurement and quality improvement
options.incorrect_rationale: Outcome measurement involves systematically tracking change in a client's performance over time using standardized tools, which has not yet occurred in this scenario.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is completing an initial evaluation with a 72-year-old man who was recently discharged home following a stroke. He reports that he is frustrated about his difficulty with grooming and cooking but is otherwise unsure of his priorities. The therapist wants to identify the client's self-perceived occupational performance problems AND measure his satisfaction with his own performance. Which standardized assessment is MOST appropriate for this purpose?
questions.correct_rationale: The Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM) is a client-centered, semi-structured interview that asks clients to identify their own occupational performance problems across self-care, productivity, and leisure, then rate both their performance and their satisfaction with performance on a 1-10 scale. This directly meets the stated purpose: surfacing client-perceived priorities AND quantifying satisfaction — something no clinician-rated ADL measure can accomplish.
questions.core_concept: The COPM operationalizes the client-centered practice principle that the client — not the clinician — is the expert on which occupational performance problems matter most and how satisfying their performance feels. OTs use it to ensure intervention goals reflect what is meaningful to the individual rather than what an observer determines is functionally deficient.
questions.explain_differently: Think of it this way: clinician-rated tools (FIM, Barthel) are like a teacher grading a student's work from the outside. The COPM hands the grading pen to the student — the client scores himself on what he finds hard and how happy he is with how he does it. Only the COPM is built specifically for that two-part, self-report job.
questions.topic: Client-Centered Occupational Performance Assessment — Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM)

options.label: A
options.text: Functional Independence Measure (FIM)
options.incorrect_rationale: The FIM is a clinician-rated measure of functional independence and burden of care; it does not capture the client's self-perception of performance or satisfaction with performance.

options.label: B
options.text: Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM)

options.label: C
options.text: Barthel Index
options.incorrect_rationale: The Barthel Index quantifies a clinician's observation of ADL independence but does not elicit the client's own priorities or satisfaction ratings.

options.label: D
options.text: Kohlman Evaluation of Living Skills (KELS)
options.incorrect_rationale: The KELS screens for basic living skills needed for community safety but is not designed to capture self-perceived performance problems or satisfaction ratings across all occupational areas.

questions.stem: The OT reflects on the 'non-compliant' label in Maria's chart and recognizes it may represent systemic barriers rather than voluntary behaviour. Which initial action BEST demonstrates a culturally safe and anti-oppressive approach as the OT begins the assessment?
questions.correct_rationale: Culturally safe practice requires the OT to actively resist deficit-focused documentation (e.g., 'non-compliant') that reflects systemic barriers rather than client character. Opening the session by inviting Maria to share her own narrative — her roles as grandmother, her community participation, her goals — enacts both anti-oppressive practice and genuine client-centredness. It disrupts the clinician-as-expert dynamic, honours self-determination, and creates the psychological safety necessary for Maria to disclose meaningful occupational priorities, including those tied to her cultural identity and community.
questions.core_concept: Cultural safety moves beyond cultural awareness to require practitioners to critically examine how power, systemic racism, and institutional bias — such as deficit labels in clinical records — shape client experiences and outcomes. Anti-oppressive OT practice centres the client's lived experience and self-defined priorities as the starting point for assessment, rather than reproducing the clinician's or institution's agenda.
questions.explain_differently: Think of Maria's chart as a rumour that arrived before she did. The rumour says she is difficult and uncooperative. A culturally unsafe response is to walk into the room already believing the rumour and asking her to defend herself against it. A culturally safe response is to put the rumour face-down on the desk and say, 'Tell me about your life — what matters to you?' Option B does exactly that: it treats Maria as the authority on her own experience instead of a problem to be explained.
questions.topic: Culture, Equity and Justice — Cultural Safety and Anti-Oppressive Practice

options.label: A
options.text: Ask Maria directly why she did not follow through with her physiotherapy sessions so the OT can address the obstacles before setting new goals.
options.incorrect_rationale: Framing the opening question around missed physiotherapy centres the clinician-defined compliance narrative rather than Maria's perspective, reinforcing the power imbalance embedded in the chart label.

options.label: B
options.text: Contact the referring surgeon before proceeding to clarify the circumstances of the non-compliance so the OT has an accurate clinical picture.
options.incorrect_rationale: Seeking the physician's account before hearing Maria's own story privileges the institutional perspective over the client's voice, which contradicts anti-oppressive and client-centred principles.

options.label: C
options.text: Set aside the deficit-focused chart language and open the session by inviting Maria to describe her life, roles, and priorities in her own words and at her own pace.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer and does not have an incorrect rationale.

options.label: D
options.text: Administer a validated standardized functional assessment to establish an objective performance baseline before discussing cultural or personal preferences.
options.incorrect_rationale: Prioritizing a standardized tool before rapport and goal-setting centres the clinician's agenda, and using an instrument not validated with Indigenous populations may itself introduce cultural bias.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is conducting a home assessment with a First Nations elder following a stroke. The elder's adult daughter is present throughout the visit and responds to nearly every question the OT poses, even when the OT addresses the elder directly. The elder remains largely quiet but makes frequent eye contact with the daughter and nods in apparent agreement. The OT is unsure how to proceed. Which action best reflects culturally safe, client-centred practice?
questions.correct_rationale: Culturally safe practice requires the OT to recognize that individualistic, dyadic communication between clinician and client is a Western construct that may not reflect the values of Indigenous or collectivist cultures, where family members appropriately speak on behalf of loved ones as an expression of relational care and collective decision-making. The elder's non-verbal cues (eye contact, nodding) indicate ongoing engagement and implicit consent to this dynamic. Adapting the assessment format to include the daughter — while remaining attentive to the elder's responses — honours the elder's cultural world-view without abandoning person-centred principles. This reflects the OT competency of cultural humility: adjusting practice to the client's context rather than expecting the client to conform to clinical norms.
questions.core_concept: Cultural safety in occupational therapy requires practitioners to recognise that mainstream clinical models of individual autonomy and direct client communication reflect Western cultural assumptions that may not align with Indigenous or collectivist values. Adapting assessment processes to honour family-centred communication styles — rather than requiring clients to conform to clinical norms — is the practical expression of this competency.
questions.explain_differently: Think of it this way: if a client grew up in a household where important decisions are always made together as a family, having a clinician push the family member out of the conversation does not feel empowering — it feels disrespectful and isolating. Cultural safety asks the OT to be a guest in the client's cultural world, not a gatekeeper enforcing unfamiliar rules. Staying in the room, watching the elder's body language, and letting the daughter co-participate is the equivalent of removing your shoes at the door — a small, respectful adjustment that signals you are safe to work with.
questions.topic: Cultural Safety and Indigenous Client-Centred Practice

options.label: A
options.text: Politely redirect all questions exclusively to the elder, explaining that professional standards require direct consent and communication from the identified client.
options.incorrect_rationale: Insisting on individualistic direct communication imposes a Western autonomy framework onto an Indigenous context and is itself a form of cultural unsafety that can rupture therapeutic rapport.

options.label: B
options.text: Pause the assessment, document that the elder demonstrates limited verbal participation, and reschedule once a formal interpreter or cultural liaison has been arranged.
options.incorrect_rationale: Conflating culturally normative family-led communication with a communication barrier or capacity deficit is a clinical error that can stigmatise the client and is not warranted by the information given.

options.label: C
options.text: Conclude the visit early and consult a social worker to verify whether the daughter holds legal power of attorney before any further assessment proceeds.
options.incorrect_rationale: Escalating to a legal-authority check is premature and unnecessary when there is no evidence of cognitive incapacity or coercion; this action pathologises a normal relational dynamic and creates an avoidable barrier to care.

options.label: D
options.text: Acknowledge the family's communication pattern as potentially culturally meaningful, continue the assessment by engaging both the elder and daughter, and observe the elder's non-verbal responses to confirm understanding and agreement.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is attending a weekly interprofessional team meeting for a client recovering from a stroke in an inpatient rehabilitation unit. Which information is MOST important for the OT to contribute to the team discussion?
questions.correct_rationale: Occupational therapy's distinct contribution to the interprofessional team is expertise in functional performance and occupational engagement. By reporting on the client's abilities and limitations in self-care, role performance, and meaningful activities, the OT provides information that no other discipline duplicates, ensuring team decisions about goals, intensity, and discharge planning are grounded in occupational function.
questions.core_concept: The OT's unique professional identity on an interprofessional team is rooted in occupation-centered practice: the OT's primary contribution is functional and occupational performance data, not medical, pharmacological, or administrative information. Understanding this scope-of-practice boundary enables effective, non-duplicative teamwork.
questions.explain_differently: Think of each team member as owning a lane on a highway. The physician owns the medical/diagnostic lane, nursing owns the physiological monitoring lane, and the OT owns the "what can this person actually do in daily life" lane. At a team meeting, each driver reports from their own lane. The OT's job is to drive the occupational performance lane — self-care, roles, meaningful tasks — because that is the information only the OT has gathered and the team cannot get it from anyone else.
questions.topic: OT's role and contribution in interprofessional team communication

options.label: A
options.text: The client's functional performance in self-care tasks and progress toward meaningful occupational roles

options.label: B
options.text: The client's current medication regimen and potential side effects affecting alertness
options.incorrect_rationale: Medication management falls within the scope of the physician, pharmacist, and nursing staff; the OT reports on how alertness affects occupational performance, not the pharmacological details themselves.

options.label: C
options.text: The client's neurological prognosis based on the most recent imaging results
options.incorrect_rationale: Interpretation of neuroimaging and neurological prognosis is within the physician's or neurologist's scope, not the OT's primary contribution to the team.

options.label: D
options.text: The client's anticipated discharge date as recommended by the attending physician
options.incorrect_rationale: Discharge date is determined primarily by the physician and case manager; the OT contributes functional readiness data that informs that decision, but does not set the timeline.

questions.stem: The OT arrives on post-operative day 2 to conduct an initial evaluation. Mabel reports she is tired and becomes anxious when asked to participate. Given her cognitive status, emotional state, and the acute care context, what is the OT's BEST initial action?
questions.correct_rationale: In acute care, OT must balance efficiency with client-centered practice. A brief interview acknowledges the patient's emotional state, builds therapeutic rapport, and identifies her occupational priorities, all of which guide evaluation focus. Observing a toilet transfer simultaneously yields high-yield data: functional cognition, hip precaution compliance, balance, and transfer technique. This approach is occupation-based, time-efficient, and directly informs discharge planning, satisfying both best-practice and acute care constraints.
questions.core_concept: In acute care OT, the initial evaluation must be simultaneously client-centered and functionally focused. Combining a brief occupational profile interview with direct observation of a meaningful ADL task is the most efficient and evidence-aligned approach, integrating rapport-building with functional performance data collection within the constraints of a short hospital stay.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the acute care OT evaluation as a two-for-one opportunity: the conversation tells you what the patient values and fears, while watching her do something real like getting to the toilet tells you whether she can actually do it safely. You learn about her mind and her body at the same time, without wasting a precious day. Deferring or running through a checklist tool ignores both the clock and the person.
questions.topic: Acute care OT evaluation approach and client-centered practice

options.label: A
options.text: Administer the full Functional Independence Measure (FIM) to establish a documented baseline before engaging in any functional tasks.
options.incorrect_rationale: The FIM is an interdisciplinary rating scale, not a client-centered OT evaluation tool, and administering it in full while the patient is fatigued and anxious does not prioritize rapport or occupational performance.

options.label: B
options.text: Conduct a brief occupation-focused interview to establish rapport and identify the patient's priorities, then observe her performance during a functional mobility task such as a toilet transfer.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer; no distractor rationale applies.

options.label: C
