options.incorrect_rationale: The MoCA screens for cognitive impairment but does not measure actual IADL performance or safety, so it cannot answer the referral question about functional independence in medication management and bill-paying.

options.label: C
options.text: Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM)
options.incorrect_rationale: The COPM captures the client's self-perception of performance and satisfaction, but this client denies any difficulty, so her self-report would under-identify deficits and would not yield objective safety data.

options.label: D
options.text: Barthel Index
options.incorrect_rationale: The Barthel Index measures basic ADL independence (e.g., feeding, bathing, transfers) and does not assess the complex IADLs — medication management and financial tasks — that are the focus of this referral.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old accountant is seen by an OT 6 weeks after a mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). He reports difficulty sustaining concentration during complex financial calculations, poor short-term memory for client details, and significant mental fatigue after 1 to 2 hours of cognitive effort. His primary goal is to return to full-time work. Which intervention is MOST appropriate at this stage of recovery?
questions.correct_rationale: At 6 weeks post-mTBI, spontaneous neurological recovery is still actively occurring. Evidence-based OT practice for this stage prioritizes compensatory strategy training — external cognitive aids (planners, checklists), task segmentation, and energy management — because these interventions directly support real-world occupational performance in the client's actual role while recovery continues. This approach aligns with the occupation-based principle of targeting the specific tasks that matter to the client (complex accounting work) rather than decontextualized remediation or premature role abandonment.
questions.core_concept: In the subacute phase of mTBI recovery, compensatory strategy training — the use of external aids, task modification, and energy management — is the first-line OT intervention because it directly supports functional occupational performance in the client's own roles while neurological healing continues. This reflects the OT principle that interventions must be occupation-centered and timed appropriately to the client's stage of recovery.
questions.explain_differently: Picture compensatory strategies as a temporary scaffold around a building under repair. The building (the brain) is actively healing on its own, but the scaffold (planner, timed breaks, task chunking) lets the client keep living and working inside it right now. Tearing down the building to build a simpler one (changing careers) or just waiting for the building to finish healing without any scaffold (remediation alone, no functional support) both leave the client unable to work in the meantime — and that directly opposes the client's own stated goal.
questions.topic: Mild Traumatic Brain Injury — Return-to-Work Intervention Selection

options.label: A
options.text: Initiate intensive computerized cognitive remediation exercises targeting attention and working memory deficits in isolation
options.incorrect_rationale: Computerized remediation has limited generalization to real-world occupational performance when used in isolation; it may be a useful adjunct, but compensatory strategies targeting the client's specific work tasks produce more immediate functional gains.

options.label: B
options.text: Teach compensatory strategies including use of a structured planner, breaking complex tasks into timed work segments, and scheduling mandatory cognitive rest breaks

options.label: C
options.text: Recommend permanent workplace accommodations including a permanently reduced caseload and avoidance of all complex financial tasks
options.incorrect_rationale: Permanent accommodations are premature at 6 weeks post-mTBI when substantial spontaneous and therapy-driven recovery is still expected; establishing permanent limitations at this stage fails to honor the client's recovery trajectory and goals.

options.label: D
options.text: Refer immediately to vocational rehabilitation for retraining in a less cognitively demanding occupation
options.incorrect_rationale: Vocational retraining in an entirely new occupation is a disproportionate response to a mild TBI at 6 weeks; the evidence-based goal is to support return to the client's existing meaningful role, not to abandon it prematurely.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is working with a 58-year-old woman recently diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis. She reports difficulty with dressing, cooking, and grocery shopping. The occupational therapist administers the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM) during the initial evaluation. What is the PRIMARY purpose of this assessment?
questions.correct_rationale: The COPM is a standardized, client-centered, semi-structured interview tool designed to detect changes in a client's self-perception of occupational performance over time. It asks clients to identify daily activities they need, want, or are expected to perform, then rate their current performance and satisfaction on a 10-point scale. This places occupational priorities in the client's voice, directly guiding goal-setting and intervention planning — the defining feature of a top-down, occupation-focused approach.
questions.core_concept: The Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM) is a top-down, client-centered outcome measure that captures the client's own perception of their performance problems and satisfaction across self-care, productivity, and leisure. It operationalizes the OT principle that intervention priorities must be grounded in what matters most to the client, not solely in clinician-observed deficits.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the COPM as a structured conversation where the client is the expert on their own life. Instead of the therapist deciding what problems matter, the client names which daily activities are most important to them and scores how well they feel they are doing and how happy they are with that performance. The therapist's job during the COPM is to listen and record — not to observe, measure, or test anything. That client-driven priority list then becomes the roadmap for the entire intervention.
questions.topic: Occupational Performance Assessment — Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM)

options.label: A
options.text: To measure upper extremity range of motion and grip strength affecting daily task performance
options.incorrect_rationale: The COPM is a client-centered interview, not a physical measurement tool; ROM and grip strength are performance component measures assessed with a goniometer and dynamometer.

options.label: B
options.text: To determine the presence and severity of cognitive impairment that may limit independent daily functioning
options.incorrect_rationale: Cognitive screening requires tools such as the MMSE or MoCA; the COPM does not assess cognitive status.

options.label: C
options.text: To identify the client's self-perceived occupational performance problems, priorities, and satisfaction across daily life areas

options.label: D
options.text: To observe and score the quality of the client's physical performance during simulated daily living tasks
options.incorrect_rationale: Observational performance assessment during task simulation is the purpose of tools such as the AMPS or FIM, not the COPM, which relies on the client's self-report.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist working in an inpatient rehabilitation unit wants to measure treatment outcomes for clients recovering from stroke in a manner that supports evidence-based practice. Which action BEST demonstrates this approach?
questions.correct_rationale: Validated, standardized outcome measures possess established reliability and validity, allowing the therapist to objectively quantify functional change from admission to discharge. Repeated administration at defined intervals (pre/post) creates a measurable data set that demonstrates intervention effectiveness, supports clinical decision-making, and meets the evidence-based practice requirement of integrating research evidence with clinical expertise and client values.
questions.core_concept: Outcome measurement is a cornerstone of evidence-based occupational therapy practice. Standardized, validated tools provide objective, reproducible data that allow clinicians to quantify client change, demonstrate the value of OT intervention, and align practice with current research evidence — all of which are required competencies under the NBCOT Excellence in Practice domain.
questions.explain_differently: Think of a standardized outcome measure as a ruler rather than a guess. Anyone using the same ruler at the start and end of treatment gets a number everyone can trust and compare — that is what makes the evidence "evidence." Narrative notes and satisfaction ratings are more like personal impressions; they may feel informative but cannot reliably show, in a defensible way, how much the client actually improved.
questions.topic: Outcome Measurement and Evidence-Based Practice

options.label: A
options.text: Document client progress using detailed narrative progress notes at each session
options.incorrect_rationale: Narrative notes capture qualitative observations but do not provide standardized, quantifiable data needed to demonstrate treatment effectiveness or compare outcomes across clients.

options.label: B
options.text: Use structured clinical observation alone to track functional improvements over the course of treatment
options.incorrect_rationale: Unstructured clinical observation is subject to bias and lacks the psychometric properties required to reliably measure and communicate change in a way that supports evidence-based conclusions.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the client to verbally rate their overall satisfaction with therapy at the end of each session
options.incorrect_rationale: Client satisfaction ratings measure perception of service quality, not functional outcomes, and do not constitute a validated measure of occupational performance change.

options.label: D
options.text: Administer a validated, standardized functional outcome measure at admission and discharge to quantify change

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is preparing for an initial assessment with a First Nations client recently discharged from hospital following a stroke. Which action BEST reflects a culturally safe approach at the opening of the session?
questions.correct_rationale: Cultural safety is achieved when the client — not the clinician — determines what is culturally safe. Inviting the client to define what matters to them and what the therapist needs to know positions the client as the authority on their own identity and lived experience. This directly enacts the principle that cultural safety shifts power toward the client, guards against stereotyping, and creates the relational foundation for a partnership built on the client's actual needs rather than the therapist's assumptions about their cultural group.
questions.core_concept: Cultural safety in occupational therapy is an outcome — experienced by the client — that results from the practitioner's ongoing self-reflection and commitment to power-sharing. It requires treating each client as the singular expert on their own cultural identity, rather than applying generalised knowledge about cultural groups, thereby avoiding stereotyping and upholding client self-determination.
questions.explain_differently: Think of cultural identity like a personal story: no book, liaison, or checklist can tell you someone else's story. The only way to know what matters to this particular client is to hand them the microphone and listen. Option B is the one action that does exactly that — it opens space for the client to speak first, which is the foundation of cultural safety.
questions.topic: Cultural safety and client-centred practice with Indigenous clients

options.label: A
options.text: Invite the client to share what is most important to them and what they would like the therapist to understand about themselves.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer; it centers the client as the authority on their own cultural identity and lived experience, which is the defining feature of a culturally safe encounter.

options.label: B
options.text: Review published literature on First Nations healing traditions before the session to prepare culturally informed questions.
options.incorrect_rationale: Applying group-level cultural knowledge to an individual client risks stereotyping and assumes homogeneity across diverse First Nations communities; cultural safety requires treating the client as the expert on their own experience.

options.label: C
options.text: Contact the hospital's Indigenous health liaison worker to learn about the client's cultural background before the session begins.
options.incorrect_rationale: Consulting a liaison to pre-determine a client's cultural identity assumes the liaison speaks for all First Nations peoples; this substitutes a third party's perspective for the client's own voice, undermining self-determination.

options.label: D
options.text: Modify the standardized assessment by removing items related to family roles and home environment to avoid potential cultural conflict.
options.incorrect_rationale: Removing assessment items without first understanding this individual client's preferences is paternalistic and may omit clinically relevant information; modifications should be driven by the client's expressed needs, not assumptions.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist needs to call the attending physician to report a sudden decline in a client's hand function observed during a morning therapy session. Which communication framework is MOST appropriate for organizing this verbal report?
questions.correct_rationale: SBAR — Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation — is a standardized verbal communication framework developed specifically for healthcare provider-to-provider handovers and urgent clinical reports. It ensures the listener receives the current problem, relevant history, the clinician's clinical interpretation, and a clear request for action in a logical, predictable sequence, reducing the risk of miscommunication or omitted information.
questions.core_concept: The SBAR framework is a structured interprofessional communication tool that organizes verbal or written handovers into four sequential components: Situation (what is happening now), Background (relevant clinical history), Assessment (clinician's interpretation), and Recommendation (action requested). It is the recognized standard for concise, time-sensitive provider communication in healthcare settings.
questions.explain_differently: Imagine handing off a relay baton in a race — the receiver needs to know exactly where you are in the race, what happened before they took the baton, how you read the situation, and what they should do next. SBAR gives every verbal handoff that same clear structure. SOAP and PIE, by contrast, are like the paperwork you file after the race — they belong in the chart, not in a phone call to a physician who needs to act quickly.
questions.topic: Interprofessional Handover Communication

options.label: A
options.text: SOAP (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan)
options.incorrect_rationale: SOAP is a written documentation format structured around the clinician's note-writing process, not a tool designed to organize urgent verbal communication between providers.

options.label: B
options.text: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation)

options.label: C
options.text: ICF (International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health)
options.incorrect_rationale: The ICF is a World Health Organization framework for classifying health and functional status; it is not a communication protocol for provider-to-provider handover.

options.label: D
options.text: PIE (Problem, Intervention, Evaluation)
options.incorrect_rationale: PIE is a written progress note format used in nursing and therapy documentation; it is not intended to structure real-time verbal communication between disciplines.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is updating an intervention protocol for adults with chronic low back pain. To ensure an evidence-based approach, the therapist reviews peer-reviewed systematic reviews, draws on five years of clinical experience with this population, and incorporates each client's stated priorities and daily activity goals. Which component of evidence-based practice is represented by incorporating each client's stated priorities and daily activity goals?
questions.correct_rationale: Evidence-based practice (EBP), as defined by Sackett and adopted in OT, rests on three equally necessary pillars: (1) best available research evidence, (2) clinical expertise, and (3) client values and preferences. Incorporating what each client prioritizes and wants to accomplish in daily life directly operationalizes the third pillar, ensuring that intervention decisions are client-centered and not driven solely by research findings or clinician judgment.
questions.core_concept: Evidence-based practice in occupational therapy integrates three pillars: best available research evidence, the practitioner's clinical expertise, and the client's own values and preferences. All three must be balanced; omitting any one — especially the client's voice — compromises both the quality and the client-centeredness of care.
questions.explain_differently: Think of EBP like a three-legged stool: research, expertise, and the client's own voice. If you leave out the leg representing what the client actually cares about, the stool tips over. When the therapist asks "what matters most to you and what do you want to be able to do?" — that is the client-values leg doing its job.
questions.topic: Evidence-Based Practice — Three Pillars (Client Values and Preferences)

options.label: A
options.text: Best available research evidence
options.incorrect_rationale: Best available research evidence refers to findings from peer-reviewed studies and systematic reviews, not to what the individual client values or prioritizes.

options.label: B
options.text: Clinical expertise
options.incorrect_rationale: Clinical expertise refers to the practitioner's accumulated professional knowledge and judgment, not to the client's own expressed goals and preferences.

options.label: C
options.text: Client values and preferences
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer — client values and preferences is the EBP pillar that centers the client's own stated priorities and goals in clinical decision-making.

options.label: D
options.text: Quality improvement data
options.incorrect_rationale: Quality improvement data refers to aggregate outcome metrics collected within a practice setting to monitor and improve service delivery, not to an individual client's stated priorities.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman is evaluated in outpatient OT 6 weeks after a right hemisphere ischemic stroke. Standardized testing confirms moderate left unilateral spatial neglect (line bisection deviation: 22 mm rightward; star cancellation: 31/54 correct). Cognition is intact (MoCA 27/30). She has mild left hemiparesis with sufficient left upper extremity function for bilateral task use. Her primary goal is to cook independently. During kitchen assessment she consistently omits left-sided burners, misses all ingredients placed to her left, and does not initiate leftward head turns without verbal prompting. The OT selects an intervention that targets the underlying attentional mechanism of neglect AND has the strongest evidence for generalization to untrained functional kitchen tasks. Which intervention BEST meets both criteria?
questions.correct_rationale: Prism adaptation (PA) therapy involves having the client perform repeated reaching movements while wearing prismatic lenses that shift the visual field approximately 10 degrees rightward. The motor-sensory recalibration that occurs during adaptation produces a leftward after-effect that directly counteracts the rightward attentional bias underlying neglect. Multiple randomized controlled trials (Rossetti et al., 1998; Serino et al., 2009; Mizuno et al., 2011) demonstrate that PA reduces neglect severity on standardized assessments and — critically — generalizes to untrained functional tasks including ADLs, a property not consistently shown by scanning or anchoring approaches. Integrating occupational performance training in the kitchen immediately following PA sessions leverages the active after-effect to reinforce meaningful task success, addressing both the impairment-level mechanism and the client's priority occupation simultaneously.
questions.core_concept: Impairment-level versus compensatory intervention selection for unilateral spatial neglect: OT practitioners must distinguish between compensatory strategies (scanning cues, anchoring) that manage neglect symptoms task-by-task without altering the underlying attentional bias, and impairment-level interventions (prism adaptation) that recalibrate the sensorimotor system and produce generalized reductions in neglect across untrained contexts. Selecting the intervention tier should be driven by the client's goals, cognitive capacity, chronicity, and the evidence base for functional generalization.
questions.explain_differently: Think of unilateral spatial neglect like a compass that is permanently stuck pointing right — the person's attention is magnetically pulled away from the left side of the world. Scanning training and anchoring cues are like putting sticky notes around the room reminding you to look left; they help in the specific spots where the notes are posted, but the compass is still broken. Prism adaptation therapy is like recalibrating the compass itself: the brain is briefly forced to correct for a rightward optical shift, and when the prisms come off, that correction overshoots leftward — temporarily resetting the attentional midline toward center. Because the mechanism is neural recalibration rather than task-specific habit, the benefit transfers to cooking, navigating the hallway, and other tasks the person never practiced with prisms on.
questions.topic: Neurological rehabilitation — unilateral spatial neglect intervention selection

options.label: A
options.text: Implement structured left-to-right visual scanning training performed directly within kitchen task practice
options.incorrect_rationale: Scanning training is a compensatory behavioral strategy that does not modify the underlying attentional bias; it requires deliberate, effortful redirection on every task and demonstrates limited generalization to novel environments or untrained tasks.

options.label: B
options.text: Apply high-contrast anchoring tape to the left edges of the stovetop, countertop, and recipe card to cue leftward attention
options.incorrect_rationale: Environmental anchoring cues are purely compensatory, confined to the specific locations where cues are placed, and do not alter the underlying perceptual-attentional impairment or generalize to other tasks or settings.

options.label: C
options.text: Provide consistent verbal prompting paired with errorless practice of left-sided item retrieval during repeated cooking sessions
options.incorrect_rationale: Errorless verbal cueing creates dependence on an external prompt, does not address the neurological attentional bias driving neglect, and evidence for generalization beyond the trained routine is lacking.

options.label: D
options.text: Initiate prism adaptation therapy and integrate kitchen-based occupational performance training as the after-effect is established

questions.stem: During a workstation visit, the occupational therapist observes that Maria uses a standard keyboard and mouse, repeatedly reaches across her desk to retrieve frequently used files, and takes no scheduled breaks. Her employer has agreed to reasonable accommodations. Maria rates work continuation as her highest COPM priority. Which combination of interventions BEST balances joint protection, energy conservation, and sustained work participation?
questions.correct_rationale: Option A simultaneously applies all three evidence-based pillars for work retention in inflammatory arthritis: joint protection (ergonomic keyboard and mouse reduce cumulative MCP and wrist stress), environmental modification (reorganising the workstation eliminates repetitive reaching that loads inflamed joints), and energy conservation (scheduled micro-breaks prevent cumulative fatigue that drives afternoon performance decline). Addressing all three concurrently is superior to any single-domain approach because each element targets a distinct but interacting barrier to occupational performance.
questions.core_concept: Effective OT intervention in inflammatory arthritis integrates joint protection, energy conservation, and environmental modification concurrently rather than sequentially. Each principle targets a different mechanism of occupational performance breakdown; omitting any one leaves avoidable barriers in place and reduces the likelihood of sustaining valued roles.
questions.explain_differently: Picture joint protection, energy conservation, and environmental modification as three legs of a stool: the stool only stands when all three are present. Providing only one or two legs still lets Maria's work performance collapse. She needs the complete structure working together simultaneously.
questions.topic: Joint protection, energy conservation, and work modification in rheumatoid arthritis

options.label: A
options.text: Ergonomic keyboard and mouse, workstation reorganisation to place frequently used items within close reach, and scheduled micro-breaks every 30 minutes

options.label: B
options.text: Bilateral rigid wrist splints worn throughout the full workday combined with referral for job retraining in a less physically demanding role
options.incorrect_rationale: Rigid wrist splints worn continuously during keyboard use impair fine motor function and do not address environmental contributors; job retraining directly contradicts Maria's stated goal of retaining her current position.

options.label: C
options.text: Immediate work cessation until inflammatory disease activity is medically controlled, followed by gradual return-to-work planning
options.incorrect_rationale: Work cessation is a last resort that violates occupational enablement principles and contradicts current evidence, which supports early worksite modification over cessation to preserve work identity and functional status in rheumatoid arthritis.

options.label: D
options.text: Ergonomic keyboard replacement only, with referral to physiotherapy for resistive hand strengthening before implementing any further workstation changes
options.incorrect_rationale: A single ergonomic change without energy conservation strategies or environmental reorganisation leaves major performance barriers unaddressed; delaying environmental modifications while awaiting strength gains unnecessarily prolongs occupational disruption and is unsupported by best evidence.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis is referred to outpatient OT. She is ambulatory with a cane, has mild bilateral upper extremity intention tremor, and reports significant fatigue by midday. Her primary concern is that meal preparation has become increasingly unsafe and exhausting. She states she frequently drops utensils, loses track of steps mid-task, and must rest before finishing. Which assessment would BEST guide OT intervention planning for this client's meal preparation difficulties?
questions.correct_rationale: The AMPS is a standardized, observation-based assessment in which the evaluator scores quality of motor skills (e.g., grip, coordination, endurance) and process skills (e.g., sequencing, adapting, pacing) as the client performs actual IADL tasks of their own choosing, including meal preparation. Because it directly observes the occupation of concern and yields skill-level scores, it pinpoints exactly which deficits — intention tremor affecting grip and coordination, or cognitive fatigue affecting sequencing — are limiting performance. This granular, task-embedded data maps directly onto intervention choices such as weighted utensils, energy conservation techniques, or environmental modification, making it the most actionable assessment for this referral question.
questions.core_concept: Assessment selection should match the clinical question: when the referral question is how and why a client's IADL performance is breaking down, a standardized performance-based assessment that observes actual task execution (such as the AMPS) yields the highest-yield, intervention-relevant data. Self-report tools establish priorities; single-construct measures quantify one symptom; performance-based tools identify the specific skill failures driving occupational dysfunction.
questions.explain_differently: Think of assessment choice like choosing the right diagnostic tool in medicine: if a doctor needs to know exactly which valve is malfunctioning, an echocardiogram beats a pain questionnaire. Here, the clinical question is not "does this patient have fatigue?" (the FSS) or "what does she care about?" (the COPM) — the question is "which specific skills are failing when she cooks?" The AMPS puts her at the stove and watches, scoring every motor and process move. That direct observation is the only way to see whether the problem is dropping a pan (motor) or forgetting to turn off the burner (process), and those two findings lead to completely different interventions.
questions.topic: Occupational Performance Assessment — IADL Assessment Selection

options.label: A
options.text: Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM)
options.incorrect_rationale: The COPM is a self-report priority-setting tool; the client has already named her priority, so the COPM would not reveal how or why her performance is breaking down during meal preparation, limiting its utility for directing specific interventions.

options.label: B
options.text: Assessment of Motor and Process Skills (AMPS) conducted in a clinic kitchen during a self-chosen meal preparation task

options.label: C
options.text: Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS)
options.incorrect_rationale: The FSS quantifies subjective fatigue impact as a single construct; it does not capture which motor or process skills are failing during meal preparation, so it cannot direct targeted intervention strategies.

options.label: D
options.text: Functional Independence Measure (FIM)
options.incorrect_rationale: The FIM was designed to measure burden of care for basic ADLs in inpatient rehabilitation settings and does not assess IADLs such as meal preparation with the granularity needed to guide outpatient intervention planning.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist working in an acute care hospital is preparing to transfer care of a client to the evening-shift therapist at the end of the day. The evening therapist is unfamiliar with the client. Which structured communication tool is specifically designed to support this type of clinical handover?
questions.correct_rationale: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) is the standardized interprofessional communication tool developed specifically to support structured, concise clinical handovers. It organizes information in a predictable sequence — what is happening now, relevant history, the clinician's interpretation, and what action is needed — reducing the risk of miscommunication or omitted critical information during care transitions. SOAP, PIE, and DAP are written documentation formats, not handover communication frameworks.
questions.core_concept: SBAR is the evidence-based verbal communication framework used for real-time care handovers and urgent communications in interprofessional healthcare settings. OTs must distinguish between documentation formats (SOAP, DAP, PIE — used for written records) and handover communication tools (SBAR — used for spoken or written transitions of care).
questions.explain_differently: Think of SBAR as a script for a quick, high-stakes phone call or shift handoff: it tells you exactly what to say and in what order so nothing critical gets left out. The other options (SOAP, PIE, DAP) are like filing systems for paper records — useful for charting, but not designed to guide a spoken conversation between two clinicians who need to transfer responsibility for a patient quickly and safely.
questions.topic: Structured Clinical Handover Communication (SBAR)

options.label: A
options.text: SOAP (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan)
options.incorrect_rationale: SOAP is a documentation format for progress notes, not a verbal or handover communication framework.

options.label: B
options.text: PIE (Problem, Intervention, Evaluation)
options.incorrect_rationale: PIE is a charting format used in nursing documentation, not a standardized handover communication tool.

options.label: C
options.text: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation)

options.label: D
options.text: DAP (Data, Assessment, Plan)
options.incorrect_rationale: DAP is a progress note documentation format, not a framework structured for real-time care handover between providers.

questions.stem: The OT is designing an intervention plan that must address Mr. G's dressing independence, Margaret's caregiver burden, and his mild cognitive impairment. When prioritizing the first intervention focus, which clinical reasoning approach is MOST defensible?
questions.correct_rationale: Scheduling adaptive dressing training during the levodopa peak window — approximately 60 to 90 minutes after the 7:00 AM dose — maximizes Mr. G's available motor capacity by reducing tremor amplitude and rigidity at the moment of skill acquisition. This creates the optimal neurological conditions for learning and consolidating new dressing techniques, directly addresses the client's stated priority, and will progressively reduce Margaret's assist demands as independence improves. A MoCA of 18 does not preclude procedural skill learning at this stage.
questions.core_concept: Evidence-based intervention sequencing in Parkinson's disease requires integrating pharmacodynamics into the therapy schedule. Motor skill acquisition is most efficient when therapy occurs during peak levodopa effectiveness ('on' time), and aligning training to this window is a fundamental OT clinical reasoning competency distinct from simply choosing an appropriate technique.
questions.explain_differently: Think of levodopa as creating a daily window when Mr. G's motor system is operating at its best — tremor quieter, muscles less rigid, movement more fluid. Trying to teach a new dressing technique outside that window is like coaching someone to shoot free throws when their hands are numb. The medication does not last all day, so the OT must plan the hardest motor learning inside that window. Everything else — caregiver support, cognitive strategies — is real and important, but the motor training has a narrow daily slot the OT cannot afford to miss.
questions.topic: Intervention sequencing and pharmacodynamic reasoning in Parkinson's disease

options.label: A
options.text: Begin with caregiver education for Margaret on safe assist techniques, because her burnout poses an immediate risk to the sustainability of the care environment.
options.incorrect_rationale: Caregiver education is an important adjunct but should not supersede the client's stated priority in a client-centered model; moreover, teaching Margaret safer assist techniques does not reduce her overall burden unless Mr. G's independence also improves.

options.label: B
options.text: Prioritize cognitive strategy training because a MoCA score of 18/30 represents the most significant barrier to learning any new adaptive technique.
options.incorrect_rationale: A MoCA score of 18/30 reflects mild, not severe, impairment; clients at this level can acquire procedural and habit-based skills with appropriate cueing, and targeting cognition before motor function ignores the modifiable pharmacodynamic advantage and the client's own goal hierarchy.

options.label: C
options.text: Address all three priorities concurrently in the first session to maximize efficiency within the limited home visit schedule.
options.incorrect_rationale: Attempting three distinct intervention priorities simultaneously fragments attention, overwhelms learning capacity in a client with mild cognitive impairment, and is inconsistent with evidence-based motor skill acquisition principles in Parkinson's disease.

options.label: D
options.text: Initiate adaptive dressing technique training scheduled during Mr. G's levodopa peak window (approximately 8:00 to 8:30 AM), because optimizing available motor function during skill acquisition directly targets his stated priority and leverages the pharmacodynamic window.

questions.stem: An OT is evaluating a 74-year-old man with moderate Alzheimer's disease in a memory care facility. He previously dressed independently but now requires full physical assistance and becomes visibly agitated during the morning dressing routine. During observation, the OT notes that when the shirt is already positioned on his torso, he can fasten the buttons without prompting. However, he cannot initiate or sequence the overall dressing task on his own. Which intervention approach is MOST appropriate for this client?
questions.correct_rationale: Backward chaining is the evidence-based choice because it directly leverages the client's preserved procedural memory: he can execute the terminal step (button-fastening) when the preceding steps are set up for him. By having staff complete all earlier steps and leaving only the final step for the client, each session ends with an independent success, which reduces agitation, preserves dignity, and reinforces a sense of competence. This approach matches intervention demand to the client's actual capacity and aligns with occupational therapy literature on maintaining functional participation in moderate dementia.
questions.core_concept: Backward chaining is an activity-grading strategy rooted in behavioral learning theory in which a task is broken into sequential steps and the client independently performs only the last step first, then progressively earlier steps as mastery grows. In clients with moderate dementia, it capitalizes on preserved implicit/procedural memory and guarantees that every practice trial ends with a successful, self-directed action — a critical principle when motivation and agitation are clinical concerns.
questions.explain_differently: Think of it like loading a dishwasher for someone who is learning: you do all the hard parts — rinsing, sorting, arranging — and just ask the person to close the door and press start. They feel capable because they finished the job. Over time you hand back earlier steps. Backward chaining works the same way: it engineers a guaranteed win at the end of every session, which is especially powerful for someone with dementia who cannot remember being successful but can still feel the emotional residue of having done something right.
questions.topic: Dementia and Cognitive Decline — ADL Intervention Selection

options.label: A
options.text: Implement backward chaining by providing full assist for all steps except the final step, which the client completes independently

options.label: B
options.text: Train care staff in errorless learning techniques so they can guide the client through each dressing step without allowing mistakes
options.incorrect_rationale: Errorless learning is a client-directed intervention targeting procedural memory acquisition and is not primarily a staff-training strategy; applying it here misidentifies where the intervention should be targeted.

options.label: C
options.text: Use forward chaining, requiring the client to independently complete the first step of the dressing sequence before staff assist with the remaining steps
options.incorrect_rationale: Forward chaining requires the client to successfully initiate the task sequence, which this client cannot do reliably; it does not leverage his preserved ability to complete a step that is already set up for him.

options.label: D
options.text: Provide a simplified picture-and-word checklist at the dressing area to cue each step in sequence
options.incorrect_rationale: Moderate Alzheimer's disease typically impairs the ability to read, interpret, and self-direct using written or pictorial checklists, making this strategy unreliable for this stage of cognitive decline.

questions.stem: At her four-week re-assessment, Maria's grip strength has improved to 4/5 and she reports she is now independent with dressing. However, she discloses that fatigue following workdays is severe enough that she has twice forgotten to turn off the stove after cooking. She continues to identify return to full-time teaching as her highest priority. What is the MOST appropriate OT response?
questions.correct_rationale: Forgetting to turn off the stove represents a safety-critical cognitive-fatigue interaction that cannot be deferred, yet removing Maria from her highest-priority occupation contradicts client-centered and occupational science principles. Option C is the only response that simultaneously addresses all competing factors: the immediate safety risk through compensatory strategies, the underlying mechanism through evidence-based post-stroke energy conservation, and Maria's priority goal through collaborative work-return planning — satisfying safety, evidence, and client-centeredness together.
questions.core_concept: When competing priorities arise — client-identified occupational goals versus identified safety risks — OT clinical reasoning must integrate both rather than sacrificing one for the other. Post-stroke fatigue management using energy conservation and cognitive compensatory strategies is an evidence-based approach that enables participation in meaningful occupation while reducing harm risk.
questions.explain_differently: Picture a three-legged stool: one leg is safety, one is fatigue management, and one is Maria's goals. Option A removes the safety leg — the stool topples. Option B removes the goals leg — it topples differently. Option D delays building any leg while waiting for someone else. Only Option C builds all three legs simultaneously, keeping the stool upright. Hard clinical questions test whether you recognize that the best answer must satisfy all constraints at once, not just the most prominent one.
questions.topic: Post-stroke fatigue — competing priorities in intervention planning

options.label: A
options.text: Prioritize Maria's self-identified goal and develop a graded plan to increase teaching days while setting meal preparation safety concerns aside until her fatigue improves naturally.
options.incorrect_rationale: Deferring an identified safety risk — two near-miss stove incidents linked to fatigue — is clinically indefensible regardless of client preference; prioritizing occupational goals does not supersede duty of care when a concrete harm pattern is present.

options.label: B
options.text: Implement cognitive compensatory strategies for stove safety (e.g., timer use, visual checklist), apply energy conservation principles to structure her workday, and collaboratively review the timeline for full-time return.

options.label: C
options.text: Advise Maria to suspend her return to work entirely until post-stroke fatigue resolves and stove safety is consistently demonstrated.
options.incorrect_rationale: Removing a client from a meaningful, high-priority occupation without a client-centered justification contradicts occupational science principles, reduces motivation and wellbeing, and treats fatigue as a passive condition to wait out rather than one that can be actively managed.

options.label: D
options.text: Refer Maria immediately to her physician to investigate fatigue as a possible medication side effect before continuing OT intervention.
options.incorrect_rationale: While physician communication may be appropriate, the OT has the clinical scope and evidence-based tools — energy conservation strategies and cognitive compensatory techniques — to address this presentation now; delaying action pending a referral could allow another unsafe incident to occur.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist begins an evaluation with a client recovering from a hip replacement by first interviewing the client about their daily routines, valued roles, and occupational priorities before observing any specific task performance or measuring range of motion. This sequence of evaluation BEST reflects which assessment approach?
questions.correct_rationale: A top-down assessment approach begins at the level of occupation, roles, and the client's own priorities — typically through an occupational profile or similar interview — before descending to examine underlying performance skills or body-function impairments. This sequence ensures the evaluation remains occupation-focused and client-centered from the outset, consistent with the OTPF-4 evaluation process and frameworks such as the Occupational Therapy Intervention Process Model (OTIPM).
questions.core_concept: Top-down versus bottom-up assessment sequencing is a foundational OT evaluation principle. A top-down approach prioritizes the client's occupational roles and priorities first, then investigates underlying impairments only as needed to explain occupational performance deficits, keeping intervention planning occupation-centered. A bottom-up approach begins with impairment measurement and infers occupational impact afterward.
questions.explain_differently: Think of it like reading a map: a top-down approach means you first look at the destination (where does this person want to go in life — what roles and routines matter to them?) before zooming in on the road conditions (the body-level impairments). A bottom-up approach does the opposite — it measures every road condition first and then tries to figure out whether the person can reach their destination. Because the therapist here starts with the client's priorities and daily life before checking joint motion, the approach is top-down.
questions.topic: Occupational therapy evaluation sequencing: top-down vs. bottom-up assessment

options.label: A
options.text: Bottom-up assessment approach
options.incorrect_rationale: A bottom-up approach starts at the performance-component level — measuring impairments such as strength, range of motion, or cognition — before considering how those deficits affect occupational performance.

options.label: B
options.text: Standardized performance testing
options.incorrect_rationale: Standardized performance testing refers to the use of normed, protocol-driven instruments to measure function; it describes the format of a specific tool, not the sequencing philosophy of beginning with occupation versus impairment.

options.label: C
options.text: Top-down assessment approach

options.label: D
options.text: Biomechanical frame of reference
options.incorrect_rationale: The biomechanical frame of reference guides intervention by addressing structural and movement deficits such as strength, endurance, and joint mobility — it is a theoretical framework, not an evaluation sequencing strategy.

questions.stem: Based on the initial assessment findings, which OT intervention approach BEST addresses Mrs. Vasquez's resistive behavior during morning ADL care?
questions.correct_rationale: Environmental modification and person-centered preparatory strategies — such as preferred music — reduce agitation in dementia by activating positive affect and reducing the threat response before a cognitively demanding task begins. Embedding consistency in the routine addresses the neurological need for predictability in Alzheimer's disease, directly targeting the antecedent of resistive behavior rather than reacting to the behavior itself.
questions.core_concept: Person-centered, preparatory, and sensory-based environmental interventions are evidence-based first-line OT strategies for dementia-related resistive ADL behaviors. They address the neurobiological and emotional antecedents of the behavior by creating psychological safety before task demands are introduced.
questions.explain_differently: Think of it like warming up a cold engine before driving. Before asking someone with dementia to do something demanding, you prime the environment with familiar, calming input — like beloved music — so their nervous system moves from a defensive to a receptive state. You are changing the conditions, not just the task.
questions.topic: Person-centered preparatory intervention for dementia-related ADL resistance

options.label: A
options.text: Recommend that nursing staff complete all ADLs for Mrs. Vasquez to minimize agitation and preserve her dignity.
options.incorrect_rationale: Withdrawing participation opportunities removes residual functional capacity and contradicts the OT principle of enabling meaningful occupational engagement at the client's current level.

options.label: B
options.text: Request a psychiatric consultation to assess whether a mood disorder is the primary contributor to Mrs. Vasquez's resistance to care.
options.incorrect_rationale: The behavior pattern is task-specific and responsive to positive sensory input, which does not support a mood disorder as the primary etiology requiring psychiatric referral as a first step.

options.label: C
options.text: Enroll Mrs. Vasquez in a group ADL skills training program to leverage peer modeling as a motivational strategy.
options.incorrect_rationale: Group ADL training requires multi-step carryover learning and novel social comprehension that exceed her current cognitive level and would likely increase rather than reduce frustration.

options.label: D
options.text: Establish a consistent, individualized morning routine that incorporates 1960s music as a preparatory activity before initiating ADL tasks.

questions.stem: In preparing Aroha's discharge plan, the OT attempts a home safety assessment but learns that Aroha's remote home has no running hot water, an outhouse rather than an indoor bathroom, and uneven outdoor terrain. Standard OT recommendations such as a shower chair and grab bars are not applicable. What is the most appropriate OT response?
questions.correct_rationale: Client-centred and anti-oppressive OT practice requires adapting assessment frameworks to the client's actual context rather than applying tools designed for urban or Western housing norms. Social determinants of health — including housing type, geographic location, and available community infrastructure — are core OT considerations. By exploring Aroha's real environment and community supports, the OT can generate practical, feasible, and respectful recommendations that support her safe return home.
questions.core_concept: Occupational therapists must recognize that standardized assessment tools and recommendations often encode assumptions about housing, resources, and infrastructure that do not apply universally. Anti-oppressive and client-centred practice requires adapting both the process and the output of assessment to the client's actual social and environmental context, particularly for clients from remote or Indigenous communities.
questions.explain_differently: Imagine trying to give someone directions using a map of a city they have never been to — the directions would be useless and possibly dangerous. Applying standard grab-bar recommendations to a home with an outhouse is the same problem: the tool was made for a different context. Option C asks the OT to put down the city map and instead walk the territory with Aroha — understanding what her home actually looks like, how she actually moves through it, and what supports already exist in her community — then build recommendations from there.
questions.topic: CEJ_JUSTICE

options.label: A
options.text: Adapt the assessment by exploring Aroha's actual daily routines, home environment, and community supports, then develop recommendations that are feasible and relevant to her real living context

options.label: B
options.text: Complete the standard home safety checklist and note individual items as not applicable due to non-standard housing conditions
options.incorrect_rationale: Applying a standard checklist without adaptation fails to generate meaningful, actionable recommendations and does not advance the client's safety or reflect her actual living context.

options.label: C
options.text: Defer the home safety component of the discharge plan, as it cannot be meaningfully completed given the non-standard environment
options.incorrect_rationale: Deferring the assessment entirely leaves a critical gap in discharge planning and does not fulfill the OT's duty to address barriers to safe community reintegration.

options.label: D
options.text: Recommend transfer to a supported care facility, as Aroha's home environment does not meet conventional safety standards for post-stroke discharge
options.incorrect_rationale: Recommending institutional placement based on housing that does not match urban norms, without exploring adaptive options or the client's preferences, imposes a deficit-based judgment and disregards the client's right to return to her community and cultural environment.

questions.stem: Which social determinants of health MOST directly affect Maggie's ability to access ongoing occupational therapy services following discharge from the inpatient rehabilitation unit?
questions.correct_rationale: Social determinants of health are the non-medical conditions — structural, economic, and social — in which people are born, live, and age. Geographic isolation (a rural reserve 300 km from the hospital) and the scarcity of culturally appropriate, accessible community OT services are the conditions most directly limiting Maggie's ability to receive ongoing rehabilitation care after discharge.
questions.core_concept: Social determinants of health are structural conditions — including geography, income, racism, and systemic inequity — that shape who can access care and benefit from it. Occupational therapists must assess these determinants as part of discharge and transition planning because high-quality inpatient care does not produce equitable outcomes if the post-discharge environment cannot support ongoing recovery.
questions.explain_differently: Think of social determinants as the road between the client and the care she needs. For Maggie, that road is 300 km long and largely unpaved — the distance from the hospital and the absence of culturally safe community services are the real barriers. Even excellent inpatient rehabilitation means little if there is no accessible, appropriate place to continue that work afterward. That gap is the social determinant doing its work.
questions.topic: CEJ_JUSTICE

options.label: A
options.text: Her age and biological sex.
options.incorrect_rationale: Age and biological sex may influence health outcomes broadly but are not the primary structural barriers shaping Maggie's access to post-discharge OT services in this scenario.

options.label: B
options.text: Her geographic location and the availability of culturally appropriate community-based services.

options.label: C
options.text: The severity of her residual neurological deficits following the stroke.
options.incorrect_rationale: Severity of neurological deficits is a clinical factor that shapes what services are needed, not a social determinant of health that shapes whether those services can be reached or accessed.

options.label: D
options.text: Her level of formal education prior to the stroke.
options.incorrect_rationale: Educational attainment is a social determinant in some health contexts but is not the most directly relevant structural barrier to accessing post-discharge OT services in Maggie's situation.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old construction worker is seen in outpatient OT 3 months after a moderate traumatic brain injury. He scores 26/30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), has intact motor function, and reports feeling fully ready to return to his previous job, expressing frustration with ongoing activity restrictions. His wife reports two recent incidents of burning food while cooking and multiple missed appointments over the past month. Structured self-awareness assessment reveals significant impaired self-awareness of deficits. His employer has requested formal functional clearance documentation. Which OT action is MOST appropriate at this point in the evaluation?
questions.correct_rationale: Performance-based functional cognition assessments (e.g., Multiple Errands Test, Executive Function Performance Test) evaluate how executive deficits actually manifest during real-world, multi-step occupational tasks — the precise information needed for return-to-work and safety decisions. The MoCA is a brief cognitive screen with a ceiling effect; it misses the subtle executive dysfunction that disrupts complex work tasks, as evidenced by the cooking and appointment failures. Critically, the client's impaired self-awareness makes self-report an unreliable source; objective performance observation directly addresses this limitation and provides defensible documentation for the employer.
questions.core_concept: Performance-based assessment is the OT gold standard when a standardized screen (e.g., MoCA) yields near-normal results yet real-world occupational failures persist. Impaired self-awareness invalidates client self-report as a primary data source, making direct observation of complex task performance essential for clinical reasoning, safety determination, and evidence-based documentation.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the MoCA as a smoke detector — useful for signaling "something may be wrong," but not the tool you use to locate or extinguish the fire. When a client scores nearly normal on the screen yet is burning food and missing appointments, the screen has told you all it can. The OT's distinct contribution is watching the client actually perform a complex, unstructured task in real time — that observation is where the functional story lives, and it is the only data source both specific enough to guide intervention and credible enough to satisfy an employer clearance request.
questions.topic: Functional cognition assessment and return-to-work decision-making after moderate TBI

options.label: A
options.text: Develop and provide a written cognitive compensation strategy program based on the near-normal MoCA score and the client's expressed readiness
options.incorrect_rationale: Initiating a compensation program before objectively establishing the nature and extent of real-world functional deficits skips a critical evaluation step and risks misaligning strategies with the client's actual performance gaps.

options.label: B
options.text: Issue a return-to-work clearance recommendation with suggested environmental accommodations, given that the MoCA score falls within the normal range
options.incorrect_rationale: The MoCA screens for gross cognitive impairment and does not validly predict performance on complex, multistep occupational tasks; issuing clearance based solely on this score in the presence of real-world functional failures would be clinically unsafe.

options.label: C
options.text: Administer a standardized performance-based functional cognition assessment, such as the Multiple Errands Test or a complex IADL task battery, to objectively characterize real-world executive function

options.label: D
options.text: Defer OT evaluation and refer the client exclusively to neuropsychology for comprehensive cognitive testing before proceeding with any OT-specific assessment
options.incorrect_rationale: Referral to neuropsychology is often collaborative and appropriate, but OT holds unique scope to assess functional occupational performance directly; deferring unnecessarily delays safety-critical information and is not the first-priority action.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist begins a new role at a community health centre serving a large Indigenous population. Which action best reflects the principle of cultural safety in occupational therapy practice?
questions.correct_rationale: Cultural safety — as distinct from cultural awareness or competency — requires the practitioner to critically examine their own values, biases, and the structural power they hold within the therapeutic relationship. Self-reflection on positionality is the foundational, ongoing act that makes it possible for clients from marginalised groups to feel genuinely safe, respected, and in control of their care. The concept originates in nursing scholarship (Ramsden) and is central to anti-oppressive OT practice; it locates responsibility with the provider, not the client.
questions.core_concept: Cultural safety is a relational and reflexive practice in which the clinician continuously examines how their own cultural background, privilege, and institutional power shape the therapeutic encounter. Unlike cultural competency (learning facts about a group), cultural safety shifts the focus from the client's culture to the clinician's self-awareness and the equitable distribution of power in care.
questions.explain_differently: Think of it this way: cultural safety is less about what you know about someone else's culture and more about what you know about yourself. Just as a good referee must understand and check their own biases rather than simply memorise the rulebook, a culturally safe OT regularly asks "How might my background, assumptions, or professional authority be affecting this person's ability to speak freely and direct their own care?" That internal audit — not a certificate or a decorated waiting room — is what makes the space genuinely safe.
questions.topic: Cultural Safety and Anti-Oppressive Practice

options.label: A
options.text: Complete a cultural competency course focused on Indigenous customs and traditional healing practices
options.incorrect_rationale: Cultural competency courses that catalogue group practices can reinforce stereotypes and suggest a fixed end-point of knowledge; cultural safety requires ongoing reflexive practice, not a one-time achievement.

options.label: B
options.text: Decorate the clinic with Indigenous artwork and symbols to signal inclusion and create a welcoming environment
options.incorrect_rationale: Using cultural symbols without meaningful structural or relational change is tokenism; it does not address power imbalances or create an environment where clients genuinely feel safe to express their needs.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask each Indigenous client to explain their cultural beliefs and practices at the start of each session
options.incorrect_rationale: Routinely asking clients to educate the clinician places an unfair burden on the client, assumes cultural identity is uniform across diverse Indigenous nations, and centres the OT's knowledge gap rather than the client's occupational goals.

options.label: D
options.text: Engage in ongoing critical self-reflection about how the OT's own cultural identity, biases, and positional power may affect interactions with clients
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer and is not a distractor.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old male is 6 weeks post-left hemisphere ischemic stroke. He presents with moderate Broca's aphasia, right hemiplegia (Fugl-Meyer Upper Extremity score 28/66; trace active wrist extension only), and mild executive dysfunction. Prior to the stroke he was a high school history teacher and is strongly motivated to return to that role. His wife reports he consistently refuses augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) devices recommended by speech-language pathology. He currently achieves independence in basic ADLs using his non-dominant left hand but is slow and easily fatigued by multi-step tasks. Which intervention plan BEST reflects current evidence-based occupational therapy priorities for this client at this point in recovery?
questions.correct_rationale: At 6 weeks post-stroke, neuroplasticity is highly active and task-specific training is the mechanism that drives cortical reorganization most effectively. Option C reflects OT's distinct scope: embedding motor retraining within occupationally meaningful, role-relevant tasks (teaching activities) rather than treating impairments in decontextualized exercise. This dual purpose — using the occupation as both the rehabilitation medium and the functional goal — is supported by current motor learning and neuroplasticity evidence. Embedding SLP-recommended communication strategies within teaching-task rehearsals also strategically addresses the client's refusal of standalone AAC by making the strategies feel integral to professional practice rather than disability-defining, increasing adherence while honoring the client's occupational identity.
questions.core_concept: Occupation-based, task-specific training is the evidence-based mechanism through which OT drives neuroplastic recovery after stroke, distinguishing it from generic motor exercise. The OT's unique contribution is selecting and grading meaningful occupational tasks that simultaneously serve as the rehabilitation medium and the functional outcome, thereby aligning the neurobiological requirements of cortical reorganization with the client's identified roles and identity.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the injured brain like a road crew rerouting traffic after a highway collapse: the crew builds the detour fastest when cars are actually trying to reach a destination people care about, not just driving laps on a test track. Having a history teacher practice gripping a dry-erase marker and tapping through a slideshow gives his brain a compelling, real destination — classroom return — that motivates the nervous system to build new routes far more urgently than squeezing a therapy putty ball. Weaving communication strategies into those same teaching rehearsals also bypasses his resistance to AAC: he is not practicing "disability tools," he is rehearsing his craft, which keeps him engaged and makes the strategies stick.
questions.topic: Stroke Rehabilitation — Occupation-Based Intervention Selection and Neuroplasticity

options.label: A
options.text: Design occupation-based upper extremity retraining using teaching-specific tasks (e.g., writing on a whiteboard, navigating presentation software, handling instructional materials) to drive neuroplasticity through task-specific practice, while collaborating with SLP to embed functional communication strategies within those same role-relevant rehearsals.

options.label: B
options.text: Initiate a modified constraint-induced movement therapy (mCIMT) protocol targeting right upper extremity motor recovery for 3 hours daily, as the neuroplastic recovery window is narrowing and restoration of hand function is the primary determinant of role resumption.
options.incorrect_rationale: mCIMT requires minimum active movement criteria (typically 10 degrees of wrist and finger extension) this client does not yet meet, and delivering motor practice as an isolated impairment protocol without occupational context misrepresents OT scope and underutilizes evidence showing that occupation-driven task specificity produces superior cortical reorganization.

options.label: C
options.text: Shift focus entirely to compensatory left-hand dominance training for ADL efficiency and refer immediately to vocational rehabilitation for alternative employment options, as moderate upper extremity impairment and aphasia at 6 weeks predict low likelihood of return to teaching.
options.incorrect_rationale: Abandoning restorative intervention at 6 weeks is premature — evidence supports continued neuroplastic gains through at least 3 to 6 months post-stroke — and prognosticating closure on the client's own identified occupational goal without attempting occupation-based recovery violates client-centered practice and introduces clinician bias.

options.label: D
options.text: Administer a full standardized assessment battery — including the Wolf Motor Function Test and Assessment of Motor and Process Skills — before initiating any treatment, to establish valid outcome baselines and an accurate recovery prognosis.
options.incorrect_rationale: Delaying treatment solely to complete a comprehensive battery wastes the active neuroplasticity window; best practice integrates ongoing standardized measurement with treatment rather than using assessment as a prerequisite gate that defers occupational intervention.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist begins working with a 58-year-old man recently discharged home following a stroke. The client states that returning to driving and managing his own finances are his most important goals. Which assessment tool is MOST appropriate for systematically identifying and prioritizing this client's self-identified occupational performance concerns?
questions.correct_rationale: The COPM is a validated, client-centered semi-structured interview in which the client identifies occupational performance problems across self-care, productivity, and leisure, then rates each for both performance and satisfaction on a 10-point scale. This process directly operationalizes client-centeredness by allowing the individual — not the clinician — to define and rank what matters most, making it the best fit when the goal is to systematically surface and prioritize the client's own concerns.
questions.core_concept: Client-centered assessment requires tools that elicit the client's own perspective on occupational performance problems and priorities rather than imposing a clinician-defined item set. The COPM exemplifies this approach by structuring a collaborative interview around the client's self-identified roles and goals across all occupational domains.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the COPM as handing the steering wheel to the client: instead of the therapist deciding which tasks to evaluate, the client names the activities that feel broken and ranks how much each one matters. The other tools on this list are clinician-driven checklists — useful for measuring how well someone performs a fixed set of tasks, but blind to what the client actually cares about. When the question is "what does THIS person most need to work on?", the client must answer it — and that is exactly what the COPM is designed to do.
questions.topic: Client-Centered Occupational Performance Assessment

options.label: A
options.text: Barthel Index
options.incorrect_rationale: The Barthel Index measures functional independence in basic ADLs (e.g., feeding, bathing, mobility) using clinician observation; it does not invite the client to identify or prioritize personally meaningful occupational goals.

options.label: B
options.text: Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM)
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer — the COPM is a validated, client-centered semi-structured interview in which the client identifies and rates occupational performance problems across self-care, productivity, and leisure.

options.label: C
options.text: Functional Independence Measure (FIM)
options.incorrect_rationale: The FIM is a clinician-rated scale measuring burden of care across 18 self-care, mobility, and cognition items; it does not capture client-identified priorities or complex IADLs such as driving or financial management.

options.label: D
options.text: Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE)
options.incorrect_rationale: The MMSE is a brief cognitive screening instrument measuring orientation, recall, and language; it does not assess occupational performance or elicit the client's occupational priorities.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman with moderate Alzheimer's disease lives with her adult daughter. The daughter reports the patient has stopped participating in meal preparation, an occupation she engaged in daily for over 50 years and still identifies as central to her role. During the OT evaluation, the clinician observes that the patient follows 2-step verbal instructions, recognizes familiar kitchen objects, and initiates stirring when handed a spoon. Which intervention approach MOST reflects evidence-based OT practice for this client?
questions.correct_rationale: The patient's observed abilities — following 2-step instructions, recognizing familiar objects, and initiating a familiar motor act when cued — indicate preserved functional capacity that can be harnessed through activity grading and errorless learning. Breaking meal preparation into 1-to-2-step segments matches task demand to cognitive capacity, while errorless learning cues (guiding correct responses before errors occur) exploit intact implicit and procedural memory. This approach is supported by dementia-specific OT evidence and upholds the profession's core commitment to maintaining meaningful participation rather than defaulting to caregiver substitution.
questions.core_concept: Activity grading and errorless learning in dementia care: OTs adapt the structure and complexity of meaningful occupations to match a client's residual cognitive-functional capacities, preserving participation in valued roles rather than excluding the person from those roles based on diagnosis alone. Preserved implicit memory and procedural initiation can be leveraged even in moderate dementia when tasks are appropriately scaffolded.
questions.explain_differently: Think of this like adjusting the difficulty setting so the game is still playable. You are not stopping her from cooking — you are restructuring the task so each step is within reach, and you guide her to succeed every time instead of letting errors accumulate. Decades of daily cooking have left strong muscle-memory traces; cuing her through a short, simplified sequence taps those traces. Taking the spoon away entirely would erase the last connection she has to an identity she built over a lifetime.
questions.topic: Dementia and Cognitive Impairment — Occupation-Based Intervention

options.label: A
options.text: Train the daughter to complete meal preparation independently, as the patient's cognitive impairment makes safe participation unrealistic
options.incorrect_rationale: This approach eliminates the patient from a deeply meaningful occupation despite demonstrated residual functional abilities, which is inconsistent with occupation-centered practice and the evidence that preserved procedural skills can be leveraged in dementia.

options.label: B
options.text: Administer the Allen Cognitive Level Screen (ACLS) to establish a cognitive level before initiating any meal preparation intervention
options.incorrect_rationale: The OT's structured task observation has already yielded sufficient functional information to guide intervention; adding a formal cognitive screen at this point delays meaningful intervention without changing the clinical picture.

options.label: C
options.text: Simplify meal preparation into 1-to-2-step sequences and use errorless learning cues to support continued participation in the task
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer and does not have an incorrect rationale.

options.label: D
options.text: Initiate repetitive practice of the full meal preparation sequence to strengthen procedural memory for the complete task
options.incorrect_rationale: Practicing the entire sequence exceeds the patient's current cognitive capacity, creating repeated failure experiences that are contraindicated under errorless learning principles and may increase frustration and disengagement.

questions.stem: During a meal observation, the OT notes that Marcus consistently ignores food on the left half of his tray and does not orient toward the therapist when approached from his left side. Visual field testing by confrontation at bedside is intact bilaterally. Which condition most accurately describes Marcus's presentation?
questions.correct_rationale: Unilateral spatial neglect (USN) is the failure to attend to, report, or respond to stimuli contralateral to a brain lesion in the absence of primary sensory or motor deficits sufficient to explain the behavior. The defining clinical discriminator from hemianopia is intact visual fields — Marcus can see to the left but his brain's attentional system fails to process left-sided stimuli. Left USN is the expected sequela of right MCA stroke, and the behavioral presentation at meals is a classic manifestation.
questions.core_concept: Unilateral spatial neglect is a perceptual-attentional disorder in which the brain fails to process stimuli on the side contralateral to the lesion despite intact sensory pathways. The critical distinction from hemianopia is that visual fields are preserved; the deficit is in attentional allocation, not sensory reception.
questions.explain_differently: A camera analogy clarifies the difference: hemianopia means the left lens of Marcus's visual camera is broken — he physically cannot capture light from that side. Neglect means both lenses work perfectly, but the brain's editing room is ignoring all the footage from the left. Because his visual fields are intact, the problem must be upstream in attentional processing, not in the sensory hardware — which is the defining feature of neglect.
questions.topic: Differential identification of left unilateral spatial neglect versus visual field deficits

options.label: A
options.text: Left homonymous hemianopia
options.incorrect_rationale: Homonymous hemianopia is a primary visual field deficit caused by damage to the visual pathway; it is ruled out here because bedside confrontation testing confirmed intact bilateral visual fields.

options.label: B
options.text: Ideomotor apraxia
options.incorrect_rationale: Ideomotor apraxia is the inability to execute learned skilled movements on command despite intact motor and sensory function; it does not explain failure to attend to one side of space during passive tasks like eating.

options.label: C
options.text: Simultanagnosia
options.incorrect_rationale: Simultanagnosia is the inability to perceive more than one object at a time and is associated with bilateral posterior parietal lesions (Balint syndrome); it does not present as lateralized inattention to one hemispace.

options.label: D
options.text: Left unilateral spatial neglect

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis reports that her morning self-care routine takes approximately 3 hours and leaves her too fatigued to fulfill her roles as a part-time administrative assistant and primary caregiver for her two school-age children. She completes all ADLs independently but rates her fatigue as 8 out of 10 by mid-morning. Her stated priority is to have enough energy remaining to engage with her children after work. Which intervention approach should the OT prioritize?
questions.correct_rationale: Energy conservation and activity pacing is the first-line, evidence-based OT intervention for fatigue in neurological conditions including MS.
