This multicomponent approach respects occupational identity, applies compensatory principles matched to the specific motor deficit, and supports meaningful engagement — the core goal of OT.
questions.core_concept: Adaptive occupation-based intervention requires accurate matching of strategies to the specific motor impairment profile. In Parkinson's disease, resting tremor abates during purposeful activity, so the priority is addressing bradykinesia and rigidity through ergonomic tool modification, postural support, and medication-timed scheduling — not tremor-dampening devices, which target a different neuromechanical deficit entirely.
questions.explain_differently: Here is the counterintuitive insight: Parkinson's resting tremor often quiets once the hands are actually doing something. So during knitting, the real enemies are slowness and stiffness, not shaking. The fix is to make the task physically easier — bigger needles, better posture, arms rested — and to do it when the medication is working hardest. That is very different from trying to weigh the tremor down, which would only help if it were a different kind of tremor.
questions.topic: OT Expertise — ADL/IADL Intervention and Meaningful Occupation

options.label: A
options.text: Schedule knitting trials during Margaret's levodopa 'on' period using large-diameter ergonomic knitting needles, with her seated in a supportive chair with bilateral forearm support on armrests.

options.label: B
options.text: Recommend that Margaret discontinue knitting and redirect her to a low-fine-motor leisure group activity that matches her current functional status.
options.incorrect_rationale: Abandoning a client's identified meaningful occupation without attempting adaptive strategies violates client-centered OT values and does not apply the available compensatory techniques that could enable participation.

options.label: C
options.text: Prescribe weighted knitting gloves to dampen hand tremor and stabilize yarn tension during the activity.
options.incorrect_rationale: Weighted devices reduce intention tremor (cerebellar origin), not the resting tremor of Parkinson's disease; moreover, Parkinson's resting tremor characteristically diminishes during purposeful voluntary movement such as knitting.

options.label: D
options.text: Suggest Margaret watch knitting tutorial videos to maintain engagement with the occupation until her tremor resolves.
options.incorrect_rationale: Passive observation does not constitute occupational participation and does not address the performance barriers; Parkinson's disease is progressive, so tremor will not resolve, making this approach both ineffective and clinically misleading.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is preparing to select an intervention for a client with mild traumatic brain injury. Before the session, the therapist searches a peer-reviewed database and reviews two recent randomized controlled trials on cognitive rehabilitation strategies. This action BEST reflects which component of evidence-based practice?
questions.correct_rationale: Evidence-based practice (EBP) rests on three interdependent pillars: best available research evidence, clinical expertise, and client values/preferences. Searching peer-reviewed databases and critically appraising randomized controlled trials is the hallmark activity for the "best available research evidence" pillar. The therapist is going to the external scientific literature — not relying on personal experience or asking the client — which uniquely identifies this action as the research-evidence component.
questions.core_concept: Evidence-based practice in occupational therapy integrates three distinct sources: (1) the best available external research evidence, (2) the practitioner's clinical expertise and reasoning, and (3) the client's individual values and preferences. Recognizing which source is being used at any point in clinical decision-making is foundational to EBP competency.
questions.explain_differently: Think of EBP like a three-legged stool. One leg is "what the science says" (research evidence), one leg is "what I know from experience" (clinical expertise), and one leg is "what the client wants" (client values). When the therapist opens a database and reads studies, they are loading weight onto the first leg — the science leg — before the stool even gets to the client's room. That is the best available research evidence, plain and simple.
questions.topic: Evidence-Based Practice — Components of EBP

options.label: A
options.text: Integrating the client's personal values and treatment preferences
options.incorrect_rationale: Client values and preferences are a distinct EBP component focused on what the client wants and prioritizes, not on consulting published research literature.

options.label: B
options.text: Applying the best available research evidence

options.label: C
options.text: Drawing on the therapist's accumulated clinical expertise
options.incorrect_rationale: Clinical expertise refers to the practitioner's own skill, experience, and professional judgment — not the act of searching external research databases.

options.label: D
options.text: Conducting an internal quality improvement audit
options.incorrect_rationale: Quality improvement audits involve systematic review of service outcomes within a setting, which is a separate process from locating external research evidence for individual clinical decisions.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist needs to communicate a sudden change in a client's functional status to the attending physician during morning rounds. Which communication framework is MOST appropriate for organizing this interprofessional verbal handover?
questions.correct_rationale: SBAR is a structured interprofessional communication framework specifically developed for verbal handovers and urgent clinical updates between healthcare providers. Each element serves the listener: Situation establishes why you are communicating now; Background provides relevant clinical context; Assessment offers the clinician's professional judgment; Recommendation specifies what action or response is being requested. This sequence ensures the physician receives complete, logically ordered information and understands exactly what the OT needs, reducing miscommunication and supporting patient safety.
questions.core_concept: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) is a standardized interprofessional communication tool used for verbal handovers and clinical updates. It organizes spoken information into a predictable sequence so that the receiving clinician can quickly grasp the current problem, understand its context, follow the speaker's clinical reasoning, and know what response is expected — reducing communication errors and supporting patient safety.
questions.explain_differently: Picture calling a colleague about an emergency. You would not hand them a written chart note — you would talk. SBAR scripts that conversation: lead with what is happening right now, give the backstory, share your professional read on it, and end with a clear ask. The other three options (SOAP, DAP, PIE) are all charting formats meant for writing in the medical record, not for speaking to a teammate in the moment.
questions.topic: Interprofessional Communication Frameworks

options.label: A
options.text: SOAP (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan)
options.incorrect_rationale: SOAP is a written documentation format for progress notes and is not designed to guide real-time verbal communication between interprofessional team members.

options.label: B
options.text: DAP (Data, Assessment, Plan)
options.incorrect_rationale: DAP is a written progress-note format commonly used in behavioral health and OT documentation; it is not a verbal handover framework.

options.label: C
options.text: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation)

options.label: D
options.text: PIE (Problem, Intervention, Evaluation)
options.incorrect_rationale: PIE is a nursing and allied health documentation structure for written records; it does not provide a protocol for organizing urgent spoken communication with another clinician.

questions.stem: The OT is educating Mabel about her posterior hip precautions before beginning ADL training. Which of the following movement combinations poses the GREATEST risk of hip dislocation for Mabel?
questions.correct_rationale: Following a posterior approach to hip surgery, the posterior joint capsule and short external rotator muscles are divided and then repaired. The three movements that most directly stress this repair and risk posterior dislocation are: hip flexion beyond 90 degrees, internal rotation, and adduction past midline. When flexion beyond 90 degrees is combined with internal rotation, the femoral head is driven directly toward the posterior capsule repair, creating the highest dislocation risk. This combination most commonly occurs during low-seated activities, crossing legs, and forward reaching while twisted.
questions.core_concept: Posterior hip precautions — no flexion greater than 90 degrees, no internal rotation, no adduction past midline — are instituted after posterior approach hip surgery to protect the repaired posterior capsule and rotator muscles while they heal. OTs must understand the biomechanical rationale for these restrictions in order to accurately educate patients and select appropriate adaptive strategies.
questions.explain_differently: Picture a door hinge at the back of the hip. The posterior approach surgery opens and repairs that hinge. Bending the hip sharply forward past 90 degrees while simultaneously twisting the leg inward is like slamming that hinge backward while it is still healing — the head of the femur pops out through the back. Every posterior precaution is designed to prevent that one dangerous direction of combined force.
questions.topic: Posterior hip precautions: biomechanical rationale and restricted movements

options.label: A
options.text: Hip extension beyond neutral while lying in a supine position.
options.incorrect_rationale: Hip extension beyond neutral is not restricted by posterior hip precautions and does not place the joint in a position of risk for posterior dislocation.

options.label: B
options.text: Hip abduction beyond 30 degrees while standing at the bedside.
options.incorrect_rationale: Abduction is not a posterior hip precaution restriction; adduction past midline is the movement restricted, making abduction relatively safe in the posterior approach context.

options.label: C
options.text: External rotation of the hip during ambulation with a walker.
options.incorrect_rationale: External rotation is not restricted following a posterior surgical approach; it is internal rotation that places the femoral head at risk of dislocation through the posterior capsule repair.

options.label: D
options.text: Hip flexion greater than 90 degrees combined with internal rotation.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer; no distractor rationale applies.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is treating a client on an acute medical unit when the client suddenly reports chest tightness and appears diaphoretic. The OT stops the session and needs to call the attending physician to communicate the change in status. Which structured communication framework is most appropriate for organizing this verbal report?
questions.correct_rationale: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) is the internationally recognized framework for structured verbal communication between clinicians in urgent or handover situations. It ensures the receiving provider receives a concise, logically ordered report: what is happening now (Situation), relevant clinical context (Background), the communicator's interpretation (Assessment), and what action is needed (Recommendation). It is designed specifically for real-time spoken exchanges, unlike SOAP, DAP, and PIE, which are written documentation formats.
questions.core_concept: SBAR is the standard interprofessional verbal communication tool used when escalating a change in client status or transferring care between providers. OTs working in medical settings must distinguish between written documentation frameworks (SOAP, DAP, PIE) and structured verbal communication frameworks (SBAR), using each in its correct context.
questions.explain_differently: Think of SBAR as a script for a phone call in a crisis — it gives the doctor everything they need in under 60 seconds: the emergency headline, the relevant history, your clinical read, and exactly what you want them to do. The other three options are filing systems for charts, not scripts for urgent spoken conversations.
questions.topic: Interprofessional Communication — Structured Verbal Handover

options.label: A
options.text: SBAR — Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation

options.label: B
options.text: SOAP — Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan
options.incorrect_rationale: SOAP is a written documentation format designed for progress notes, not a verbal handover tool for urgent provider-to-provider communication.

options.label: C
options.text: DAP — Data, Assessment, Plan
options.incorrect_rationale: DAP is a written clinical documentation structure used for session notes and is not designed to organize urgent verbal communication between team members.

options.label: D
options.text: PIE — Problem, Intervention, Evaluation
options.incorrect_rationale: PIE is a nursing-origin written charting format and does not serve the function of structured real-time verbal escalation to a physician.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is beginning intervention with a 58-year-old client recovering from a mild stroke. The therapist wants to identify which daily activities are most meaningful to the client and to measure the client's own perception of their current performance and satisfaction in those activities. Which standardized assessment BEST aligns with this purpose?
questions.correct_rationale: The COPM is a semi-structured, client-centered interview in which the client identifies occupational performance problems across self-care, productivity, and leisure, then rates their own perceived performance and satisfaction on a 1–10 scale. This dual focus on client-identified priorities and subjective self-rating makes it the assessment that most directly matches the therapist's stated purpose.
questions.core_concept: Client-centered assessment is a foundational OT principle in which the client — not the clinician — identifies and prioritizes the occupational performance problems that matter most to them. The COPM operationalizes this principle by combining a structured interview to surface meaningful activities with self-rated scales for performance and satisfaction, yielding both a goal-setting tool and an outcome measure.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the COPM as handing the "expert" role to the client: instead of the therapist deciding which tasks to evaluate, the client tells the therapist what daily activities they struggle with and care about most, then scores how well they think they are doing and how happy they are with that performance. No other option in this list gives the client that voice.
questions.topic: Standardized Occupational Performance Assessment — Client-Centered Outcome Measures

options.label: A
options.text: Functional Independence Measure (FIM)
options.incorrect_rationale: The FIM is a clinician-rated scale measuring independence across 18 motor and cognitive tasks; it does not capture client-identified priorities or subjective satisfaction with performance.

options.label: B
options.text: Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM)
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer.

options.label: C
options.text: Assessment of Motor and Process Skills (AMPS)
options.incorrect_rationale: The AMPS uses structured observation to score motor and process skill quality during pre-selected ADL tasks; it does not elicit client-identified occupational priorities or satisfaction ratings.

options.label: D
options.text: Barthel Index
options.incorrect_rationale: The Barthel Index is a clinician-completed ordinal scale of ADL independence that yields a total score; it does not solicit the client's perspective on meaningful activities or personal satisfaction.

questions.stem: On the first day of OT evaluation, the treating occupational therapist wants to identify Mr. Okafor's self-perceived occupational performance priorities and satisfaction ratings. Which assessment approach is MOST appropriate given his mild-to-moderate expressive aphasia with preserved receptive language?
questions.correct_rationale: The COPM is the gold-standard tool for identifying client-identified occupational performance priorities and is central to client-centered OT practice. However, its standard verbal interview format is contraindicated with expressive aphasia. Adapting administration using picture-based activity menus and visual rating scales (consistent with augmentative and alternative communication principles) preserves the tool's client-centered intent while accommodating Mr. Okafor's communication profile. His preserved receptive language means he can process options presented to him and indicate responses non-verbally.
questions.core_concept: Standardized assessment adaptation for communication impairment: When a client's communication profile precludes standard administration of a validated tool, occupational therapists are ethically and clinically obligated to adapt administration format while preserving construct validity, rather than substituting an entirely different tool that does not measure the same construct.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the assessment tool as a measuring cup. The COPM is the right cup for measuring client priorities. Mr. Okafor's aphasia does not change what you need to measure; it only changes what language you use to gather the information. Swapping to a different tool entirely (SIS or FIM) would be like measuring flour when the recipe calls for sugar. You would be using the wrong instrument for the wrong construct.
questions.topic: Assessment selection and adaptation for clients with aphasia

options.label: A
options.text: Administer the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM) using the standard verbal interview format
options.incorrect_rationale: The standard COPM verbal interview requires the client to generate and verbalize priority areas independently, which is not feasible for a client with expressive aphasia and would yield invalid results.

options.label: B
options.text: Administer the Stroke Impact Scale (SIS) as a written self-report questionnaire to the patient
options.incorrect_rationale: The SIS measures perceived stroke impact across multiple domains but does not capture client-identified occupational performance priorities or self-rated satisfaction, and a written format does not address expressive aphasia.

options.label: C
options.text: Administer the COPM adapted with picture-supported communication boards and visual analog rating scales

options.label: D
options.text: Use structured FIM re-assessment through performance-based observation to infer the patient's priorities
options.incorrect_rationale: The FIM is a clinician-rated measure of functional independence level and does not assess or infer client-identified occupational priorities or self-efficacy.

questions.stem: Based on Mr. Delgado's FIM data showing minimal functional gains and the OT's review of current systematic review evidence, what is the OT's BEST next step in his care?
questions.correct_rationale: Evidence-based practice requires integrating the best available research evidence with clinical outcome data and individual client factors. The FIM reveals a functional plateau under the current compensatory approach, and the systematic review directly supports task-specific training with graded repetition for clients with Mr. Delgado's profile. Modifying the treatment plan to align with this evidence is the appropriate professional response and reflects both quality improvement and outcome-driven clinical decision-making.
questions.core_concept: Evidence-based practice in OT integrates current best research evidence with standardized outcome measurement and client-specific factors to guide treatment planning. When outcome data indicate insufficient progress, the clinician is professionally obligated to revise the intervention approach rather than continue a plan that is not producing meaningful change.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the FIM as the OT's report card on the intervention — and right now the grade is failing. If you also know from research that a different teaching strategy works better for this type of student, the right move is to switch strategies, not to keep using the same one and hope something changes. Clinging to an approach that both the data and the evidence argue against is not reflective practice; it is inertia.
questions.topic: Evidence-Based Practice and Outcome-Driven Plan Modification

options.label: A
options.text: Continue the compensatory approach for two additional weeks to allow more time for the current plan to demonstrate effect.
options.incorrect_rationale: Persisting with an approach that outcome data show is ineffective, without incorporating available evidence, does not reflect evidence-based or quality improvement practice.

options.label: B
options.text: Discontinue occupational therapy services and refer Mr. Delgado to home health, given the plateau in functional gains.
options.incorrect_rationale: A plateau under the current approach does not indicate discharge readiness; the client has unmet functional goals and evidence supports a more effective alternative intervention.

options.label: C
options.text: Request a physiatrist consultation to evaluate whether Mr. Delgado's neurological status has changed before making any modifications to the intervention plan.
options.incorrect_rationale: A neurological consultation is not indicated without clinical signs of neurological change; the OT holds professional authority and responsibility to modify intervention approaches based on outcome data and best evidence.

options.label: D
options.text: Revise the treatment plan to incorporate task-specific training with graded repetition, consistent with the current systematic review evidence.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer and does not require an incorrect rationale.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist begins working with clients from a cultural background different from their own. Which action best reflects the principle of cultural humility in OT practice?
questions.correct_rationale: Cultural humility is a lifelong, self-reflective process in which the practitioner continuously examines their own assumptions and biases, remains positioned as a learner relative to the client's lived experience, and explicitly acknowledges the power differential that exists in the therapeutic relationship. Option B captures all three components — self-reflection, openness to client-led learning, and power-awareness — which together constitute culturally safe practice in OT.
questions.core_concept: Cultural humility is the OT competency of maintaining a continuous, critical self-examination of one's own values, biases, and social position, paired with genuine openness to each client's unique cultural identity. Unlike cultural competence — which can imply mastery of a fixed body of knowledge — cultural humility treats cultural learning as an ongoing relational process that centers the client as the expert on their own experience.
questions.explain_differently: Think of cultural competence as passing a driver's test once and assuming you now know every road — it sets a finish line. Cultural humility is more like committing to be a thoughtful driver for life: you check your mirrors constantly, adjust to new conditions, and never assume you have seen every situation. With each client, the therapist shows up curious rather than certain, and is honest that professional authority can itself shape the interaction — so that power gap is named and actively managed, not ignored.
questions.topic: Cultural Humility and Culturally Safe Practice in Occupational Therapy

options.label: A
options.text: Engage in ongoing self-reflection about personal biases, remain open to learning from each client, and acknowledge the power imbalance inherent in the therapeutic relationship.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer and represents the defining features of cultural humility.

options.label: B
options.text: Complete a cultural competency certificate course and apply the learned cultural norms consistently to all clients who share that background.
options.incorrect_rationale: Applying group-level cultural norms uniformly risks stereotyping and reflects a static competency-as-endpoint model, rather than the ongoing individualized reflection that defines cultural humility.

options.label: C
options.text: Refer all culturally sensitive decisions to a professional interpreter so the therapist avoids imposing personal assumptions.
options.incorrect_rationale: Delegating all cultural decision-making to an interpreter is an avoidance strategy, not cultural humility; it removes the therapist from the reflective process and can undermine direct therapeutic rapport.

options.label: D
options.text: Focus exclusively on the client's biomedical diagnosis and functional performance goals to maintain clinical objectivity.
options.incorrect_rationale: Excluding cultural context from assessment and goal-setting contradicts client-centred and anti-oppressive practice, as it ignores social determinants and the client's lived experience.

questions.stem: In occupational therapy, cultural safety is BEST described as:
questions.correct_rationale: Cultural safety — a concept originating from Maori nursing scholar Irihapeti Ramsden — is defined by the recipient's experience, not the provider's intentions. It requires that clients feel respected, safe from discrimination, and free from having the therapist's cultural norms imposed upon them. Critically, whether an interaction is culturally safe is determined by the client, making it distinct from cultural competence or awareness, which focus on the practitioner's skill set.
questions.core_concept: Cultural safety is a practice outcome centred on the client's experience of respect, dignity, and freedom from disempowerment within the therapeutic relationship. It differs from cultural awareness (knowing about other cultures) and cultural competence (acquiring skills) because it shifts accountability to the practitioner's attitudes, power, and impact — and it is always judged by the recipient, not the provider.
questions.explain_differently: Think of cultural safety less like a checklist the OT completes and more like a report card the client fills out. The OT does not get to decide the interaction was "safe" — the client does. If a client leaves feeling judged, dismissed, or pressured to abandon their own values to receive care, cultural safety was not achieved, regardless of how knowledgeable or well-meaning the therapist was.
questions.topic: Cultural Safety — Definition and Client-Centred Accountability

options.label: A
options.text: The therapist's knowledge of a client's cultural traditions, beliefs, and practices
options.incorrect_rationale: Knowing about a client's culture describes cultural awareness or sensitivity — important foundations, but not the defining feature of cultural safety, which centres the client's lived experience rather than the therapist's knowledge base.

options.label: B
options.text: An environment in which clients do not feel disempowered, demeaned, or alienated by the therapist's attitudes, assumptions, or actions
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer and requires no distractor rationale.

options.label: C
options.text: Standardising intervention protocols to ensure all clients from diverse backgrounds receive identical treatment
options.incorrect_rationale: Standardising care to deliver identical treatment can erase meaningful cultural and individual differences; it reflects procedural uniformity, not cultural safety, and may reproduce rather than reduce inequity.

options.label: D
options.text: Selecting assessment tools that have been normed on the client's cultural or ethnic group
options.incorrect_rationale: Using culturally normed tools is one component of culturally responsive assessment practice but is a specific strategy, not the definition of cultural safety as a concept.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist working in an urban Indigenous health centre reviews the clinic's intake forms and intervention protocols to identify practices that may be discriminatory or alienating to Indigenous clients. The goal is to ensure that all clients feel respected and safe to engage authentically in care. This process MOST directly reflects which principle?
questions.correct_rationale: Cultural safety is an outcome-oriented framework, developed from Maori nursing scholarship, that centres the experience of the client: care is culturally safe when the recipient does not experience racism, discrimination, or the undermining of their cultural identity. Achieving it requires providers and organizations to critically examine power dynamics, historical context, and systemic practices — exactly what the therapist is doing by auditing intake forms and protocols for discriminatory elements.
questions.core_concept: Cultural safety is distinct from cultural awareness or competence in that it shifts accountability from the individual provider's knowledge level to the structural and relational environment of care — asking whether the client, particularly from an Indigenous or marginalized community, experiences the interaction as free from discrimination and power imbalance. It demands organizational-level self-examination, not only personal skill development.
questions.explain_differently: Think of it this way: cultural awareness is noticing differences exist, cultural competence is the therapist building personal skills, but cultural safety asks a completely different question — does the client actually feel safe and unhurt by the encounter? The therapist in this scenario is acting like a building inspector, checking the structure itself (forms, protocols) for hazards that could make clients feel unwelcome or harmed, regardless of any individual therapist's good intentions. That structural audit is the hallmark of cultural safety work.
questions.topic: Cultural Safety and Indigenous Health in Occupational Therapy Practice

options.label: A
options.text: Cultural awareness
options.incorrect_rationale: Cultural awareness refers to recognizing that cultural differences exist and may affect interactions, but it does not address the structural examination of discriminatory practices or the creation of safe care environments.

options.label: B
options.text: Cultural humility
options.incorrect_rationale: Cultural humility describes an ongoing personal practice of self-reflection and acknowledging the limits of one's own cultural perspective; it is provider-centred rather than focused on removing institutional barriers to client safety.

options.label: C
options.text: Cultural safety

options.label: D
options.text: Cultural competence
options.incorrect_rationale: Cultural competence refers to acquiring knowledge, skills, and attitudes to work effectively across cultures, but it is typically framed as a static provider achievement and does not specifically address organizational practices that create or remove discrimination.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist needs to phone the attending physician to report that a client recovering from a stroke has experienced a sudden, significant decline in right upper extremity function during the morning session. Which communication framework should the OT use to organize this verbal report?
questions.correct_rationale: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) is the evidence-based, standardized framework designed specifically for urgent verbal and telephone communication between healthcare providers. It ensures the receiving clinician quickly understands what is happening (Situation), why it matters in context (Background), the OT's clinical interpretation (Assessment), and what action is being requested (Recommendation). This structure reduces miscommunication risk in time-sensitive interprofessional handovers.
questions.core_concept: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) is the internationally recognized standard for structured verbal and telephone communication between interprofessional team members, particularly when a clinical concern requires timely action. OTs use SBAR to communicate efficiently across disciplines, ensuring critical information is conveyed in a predictable sequence that supports patient safety.
questions.explain_differently: Think of SBAR as a pre-flight checklist for a phone call: before you dial, you organize exactly what is wrong right now, what led up to it, what you think it means, and what you need the physician to do. This four-part script prevents the common problem of a clinician calling with vague concerns — the physician knows within seconds why the call is urgent and what response is expected, which speeds up decision-making and reduces the chance of something being missed.
questions.topic: Interprofessional Communication Frameworks

options.label: A
options.text: SOAP — present Subjective findings, Objective measurements, Assessment, and Plan in sequence
options.incorrect_rationale: SOAP is a written documentation format used for progress notes and medical records, not a framework designed for structured verbal communication with another provider.

options.label: B
options.text: COAST — organize the report using Client, Occupation, Assistance, Supervision, and Time
options.incorrect_rationale: COAST is a goal-writing framework used to construct measurable occupational therapy goals, not a tool for interprofessional clinical communication.

options.label: C
options.text: DAP — communicate using Data, Assessment, and Plan
options.incorrect_rationale: DAP is an alternative written charting format for therapy notes; it lacks a dedicated prompt for the clinician to make an explicit recommendation, making it less suited for urgent verbal handovers.

options.label: D
options.text: SBAR — structure the message around Situation, Background, Assessment, and Recommendation

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is conducting a home assessment for a 68-year-old First Nations woman recently discharged after a hip replacement. The client lives with her adult daughter and several grandchildren in a rural community. After completing a standardized home safety checklist, the therapist presents a home modification plan that includes grab bars, a raised toilet seat, and rearranged furniture. The client nods politely throughout but asks no questions. The daughter, who is present, says, "We will need to discuss this with the rest of the family before anything changes in the house." What is the most appropriate next step for the occupational therapist?
questions.correct_rationale: Pausing and scheduling an inclusive follow-up demonstrates cultural safety and authentic client-centred practice. The daughter's statement signals that collective family deliberation is culturally meaningful, not a logistical barrier. The client's polite nodding cannot be assumed to represent informed agreement; in many Indigenous and collectivist cultural contexts, deference or silence during a clinical encounter reflects social norms rather than genuine consent. Proceeding without family input would produce a plan the household is unlikely to adopt and would undermine the therapeutic relationship.
questions.core_concept: Cultural safety in occupational therapy requires recognising that decision-making authority may rest with a family or community unit rather than the individual alone, particularly for many Indigenous clients. Client-centred practice therefore means adapting the pace, structure, and participants of care planning to align with the client's cultural values — not just their verbal responses in the clinical moment.
questions.explain_differently: Picture the plan as a contract: a polite nod in a formal, unfamiliar encounter is not the same as a signature. For this family, "talking it over together" is not a delay before the decision — it is the decision-making process itself. The therapist's role is to step into that process respectfully, not to work around it. Scheduling the follow-up is the clinical action; everything else is just paperwork filed too early.
questions.topic: Cultural safety and collectivist decision-making in Indigenous client care

options.label: A
options.text: Pause finalising the plan, schedule a follow-up that includes relevant family members, and open the meeting by asking what the family's priorities and concerns are.

options.label: B
options.text: Explain that the modifications are medically necessary for fall prevention and should be implemented before the next clinic appointment.
options.incorrect_rationale: Framing clinical urgency as a reason to override the family's process is paternalistic and culturally unsafe; it prioritises the therapist's timeline over the client's right to collective decision-making.

options.label: C
options.text: Document that the client acknowledged the plan and submit the modification request, noting the family will review on their own.
options.incorrect_rationale: Interpreting polite nodding as informed consent misreads a common cultural communication style and produces inaccurate documentation that does not reflect the client's genuine agreement.

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the daughter to share the family's main concerns right now so the assessment visit can be completed in one session.
options.incorrect_rationale: Pressing the family to condense their decision-making into the current visit for efficiency imposes the therapist's schedule over the family's cultural process and does not create genuine space for participation.

questions.stem: After four weeks of OT intervention, Maria demonstrates consistent morning self-care and prepares one meal daily. She reports improved mood and asks for immediate referral to a work-readiness program, stating 'I feel ready.' The OT notes that Maria continues to endorse fatigue and difficulty sustaining concentration beyond 20 minutes. Which action BEST reflects clinical reasoning that balances client autonomy with professional responsibility?
questions.correct_rationale: Client self-report of readiness is valuable but insufficient as a sole basis for clinical recommendations, particularly in MDD where insight into limitations may be impaired and objective deficits in concentration persist. Prior to recommending progression to work-readiness programming, the OT should administer a standardized work capacity or functional evaluation to objectively document current performance levels, identify residual barriers, and produce an evidence-based recommendation. This approach integrates client-centered values with professional duty — it neither dismisses Maria's readiness nor accepts self-report alone as sufficient evidence.
questions.core_concept: Clinical reasoning for occupational role transition requires the OT to integrate client-reported readiness with objective standardized assessment findings. Client self-determination is respected as a priority while professional judgment ensures that recommendations are evidence-based, safe, and grounded in documented functional performance.
questions.explain_differently: Maria feeling ready is important data — but it is one instrument on the dashboard, not the whole panel. An OT is like a co-pilot: the client chooses the destination, but the OT uses the instruments (standardized assessments) to check the fuel level and engine status before clearing takeoff. Skipping the instrument check and trusting only the pilot's confidence risks a mid-flight failure at the worst possible time.
questions.topic: Clinical reasoning for occupational role transition and return-to-work readiness

options.label: A
options.text: Refer Maria immediately to the work-readiness program to honor her autonomy and capitalize on her motivation.
options.incorrect_rationale: Respecting autonomy is essential, but professional responsibility requires supplementing client self-report with objective data before a clinical recommendation, particularly when concentration deficits persist.

options.label: B
options.text: Administer a standardized work capacity or functional evaluation before recommending progression to the work-readiness program.

options.label: C
options.text: Discharge Maria from OT services because she has achieved her self-care goals and demonstrates motivation for the next step.
options.incorrect_rationale: Discharge is premature; Maria has not yet achieved her primary goal of work-readiness, and objective functional deficits in concentration remain unresolved.

options.label: D
options.text: Continue IADL-focused intervention and defer work-readiness discussion until Maria can demonstrate 60 minutes of sustained attention.
options.incorrect_rationale: Applying an arbitrary attention threshold ignores the value of standardized work capacity tools that can assess multidimensional functional readiness holistically rather than by a single performance criterion.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist completes a cognitive assessment with a client recovering from a mild stroke. The client clearly states they do not want their adult son informed of any cognitive deficits identified during the assessment. Later that afternoon, the son telephones the unit and asks the OT directly about the assessment results. Which response by the OT is most appropriate?
questions.correct_rationale: A competent client has the legal and ethical right to control who receives their health information. When the client has explicitly withheld consent for disclosure to a specific individual, no clinician may share that information with that person, regardless of family relationship. The OT must decline to disclose and may encourage the client to share information with their son if they choose to do so.
questions.core_concept: Client confidentiality and information consent: occupational therapists are bound by professional and legal obligations (e.g., HIPAA in the US, PHIPA in Canada) to protect client health information. A competent client's explicit non-disclosure instruction takes precedence over family relationships or assumed caregiver need.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the client's health information as belonging to the client, not to the healthcare team. The OT is only a custodian of that information. Unless the client has given permission — or a legal exception applies (e.g., imminent safety risk) — the OT has no authority to hand that information to anyone, including a well-meaning family member. The son asking nicely on the phone changes nothing about who owns the information.
questions.topic: Client Confidentiality and Consent for Information Disclosure

options.label: A
options.text: Share the results with the son because he is likely the primary caregiver after discharge.
options.incorrect_rationale: Caregiver role does not override a competent client's explicit request for confidentiality; sharing would violate the client's right to privacy.

options.label: B
options.text: Provide a general update to the son without disclosing the specific cognitive findings.
options.incorrect_rationale: Offering any portion of undisclosed assessment information still breaches the client's confidentiality directive, regardless of how vague the update is.

options.label: C
options.text: Decline to share the assessment information and respect the client's explicit request for confidentiality.

options.label: D
options.text: Transfer the call to the supervising physician so a physician can decide whether to disclose the findings.
options.incorrect_rationale: Delegation does not resolve the ethical issue; the client's confidentiality directive applies to all members of the care team, not just the OT.

questions.stem: An OT is consulted in a memory care unit regarding a 74-year-old retired military officer with moderate Alzheimer's disease. Staff report he becomes increasingly combative during morning dressing, resisting all caregiver assistance. His family states he maintained a strict, self-directed dressing routine every morning for over 40 years. Cognitive screening confirms significant episodic memory impairment but relatively intact motor sequencing. Which intervention should the OT prioritize first?
questions.correct_rationale: In Alzheimer's disease, procedural (implicit) memory — the neural encoding of overlearned motor sequences — is preserved significantly longer than episodic and declarative memory. This client's 40-year morning routine is encoded as procedural memory. By replicating his established dressing sequence and cueing self-initiation at each step rather than providing physical assistance, the OT activates intact neural pathways, reduces cognitive demand, preserves autonomy, and directly addresses the behavioral disturbance caused by routine disruption. This aligns with person-centered, occupation-based intervention grounded in cognitive neuroscience.
questions.core_concept: Procedural (implicit) memory is selectively preserved in moderate Alzheimer's disease. Occupational therapists leverage this principle by structuring ADL routines to match a client's lifelong, overlearned patterns, which activates intact memory systems, supports functional independence, and reduces behavioral disturbance — a core strategy in dementia-specific OT intervention.
questions.explain_differently: Think of procedural memory as "autopilot." Even as Alzheimer's erases names and recent events, the brain's motor-habit system often still holds a deeply practiced sequence intact — like a soldier who has buttoned his uniform thousands of times. If caregivers interrupt or reorder that sequence, the autopilot crashes and agitation results. Restoring the familiar order and stepping back lets the autopilot take over, keeping the client calm and capable without any new learning required.
questions.topic: Dementia — procedural memory, person-centered ADL intervention, behavioral disturbance management

options.label: A
options.text: Train caregivers to use a hand-over-hand guidance technique to complete dressing efficiently and reduce the duration of the interaction
options.incorrect_rationale: Hand-over-hand guidance overrides the client's self-initiation, reduces perceived autonomy, and increases rather than decreases agitation in clients with preserved motor sequencing ability.

options.label: B
options.text: Recommend a transition to adaptive clothing with hook-and-loop fasteners to minimize caregiver handling time during dressing
options.incorrect_rationale: Adaptive clothing addresses task simplification at the equipment level but does not address the root cause of agitation, which is disruption of the client's overlearned procedural routine.

options.label: C
options.text: Reschedule dressing sessions to early afternoon when the client is typically more cooperative
options.incorrect_rationale: There is no clinical evidence of late-day confusion (sundowning) presented in this scenario; time-shifting without addressing the routine mismatch does not resolve the behavioral disturbance.

options.label: D
options.text: Restructure the dressing routine to replicate the client's lifelong sequence and allow maximum self-initiation at each step
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer; the incorrect rationale does not apply.

questions.stem: The OT documented a TSK-17 score of 48/68 for Marcus. What does the Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia specifically measure?
questions.correct_rationale: The Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia (TSK) is a validated self-report measure designed specifically to quantify fear of movement and re-injury (kinesiophobia) in individuals with musculoskeletal pain. Higher scores indicate greater fear of movement. It is a psychosocial outcome measure, distinct from disability indices and performance-based functional assessments.
questions.core_concept: The Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia (TSK) is a standardized psychosocial outcome measure targeting kinesiophobia — fear of movement and re-injury. Distinguishing it from disability measures (ODI, RMDQ) and performance tools (FCE) is essential for selecting the right assessment when the clinical hypothesis involves fear-avoidance as a barrier to recovery.
questions.explain_differently: The TSK is like a thermometer that reads how afraid someone is of moving — it does not measure how much they hurt or how much they can lift, but how scared they are that moving will hurt or hurt them again. That makes it a completely different kind of tool from a disability questionnaire or a lifting test.
questions.topic: Standardized assessment tools — Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia

options.label: A
options.text: An individual's fear of movement and re-injury related to musculoskeletal pain.

options.label: B
options.text: The degree of functional disability caused by low back pain in daily activities.
options.incorrect_rationale: This describes the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) or Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire, which measure activity limitation, not fear of movement.

options.label: C
options.text: An individual's safe maximum lifting capacity across standardized work tasks.
options.incorrect_rationale: Safe lifting capacity is measured through performance-based tools such as a Functional Capacity Evaluation, not through a self-report psychological measure.

options.label: D
options.text: The level of pain catastrophizing and depression associated with chronic pain.
options.incorrect_rationale: Pain catastrophizing is specifically measured by the Pain Catastrophizing Scale (PCS), and depression by tools such as the PHQ-9; the TSK focuses specifically on fear of movement and re-injury.

questions.stem: During the initial OT evaluation on post-stroke day 2, which approach BEST supports gathering accurate occupational performance data from Mrs. Chen given her communication profile?
questions.correct_rationale: Observation of actual task performance is the most valid and reliable method for assessing occupational performance in acute care. For a patient with Broca's aphasia and preserved auditory comprehension, the OT adapts communication by using gesture, demonstration, and yes/no questions while directly observing how Mrs. Chen executes a functional task. This yields real performance data — including motor quality, safety, compensatory strategies, and affect — that chart review cannot capture.
questions.core_concept: Observation-based, task-embedded assessment is the occupational therapy standard for evaluating performance capacity. When verbal communication is impaired, OTs adapt assessment methods using alternative communication strategies rather than deferring or substituting proxy data.
questions.explain_differently: Think of it like evaluating whether someone can safely drive — you cannot determine that from a written chart or a verbal quiz alone; you must watch them behind the wheel. With aphasia, the OT simply adjusts how they communicate during that direct observation, not whether they observe at all.
questions.topic: Aphasia-adapted occupational performance assessment in acute care

options.label: A
options.text: Complete the Functional Independence Measure (FIM) ratings using nursing documentation and chart review only, to avoid distressing the patient with direct interaction.
options.incorrect_rationale: Proxy-based and chart-only assessment systematically underestimates or misrepresents actual performance capacity because it lacks direct observation of the patient executing functional tasks.

options.label: B
options.text: Observe Mrs. Chen performing a brief functional task such as face washing while using yes/no questions, gesture cues, and demonstration to guide interaction and gather performance data.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer; it directly observes occupational performance while adapting communication to the patient's aphasia profile.

options.label: C
options.text: Defer formal occupational performance assessment until the speech-language pathologist has cleared Mrs. Chen for verbal participation in standardized testing.
options.incorrect_rationale: OT evaluation does not require SLP clearance before proceeding; deferral in acute care delays time-sensitive intervention and is not supported by evidence-based practice.

options.label: D
options.text: Administer a standardized verbal cognitive screen using full verbal instructions before initiating any functional assessment to rule out cognitive impairment.
options.incorrect_rationale: Verbal-instruction-dependent cognitive screens are invalid for patients with Broca's aphasia and will yield unreliable results; adapted communication methods must be used before drawing conclusions about cognition.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist works on an inpatient stroke rehabilitation unit and uses the Functional Independence Measure (FIM) to track client progress. During the quarterly quality improvement meeting, the data analyst reports that the unit's average FIM efficiency score for clients with stroke is 15% below the national benchmark for comparable facilities. The rehabilitation director asks the occupational therapist to propose the most appropriate next step. Which action should the occupational therapist recommend FIRST?
questions.correct_rationale: Root-cause analysis is the evidence-based first step in any quality improvement cycle (e.g., the PDSA model). Before selecting or implementing any corrective action, the team must systematically examine the contributing factors—case mix complexity, staffing ratios, therapy intensity, documentation accuracy, and discharge timing—to determine whether the gap reflects a true practice deficiency or a confounding variable. Acting on an unexplained gap without investigation risks implementing solutions that are misaligned with the actual problem, wasting resources, or inadvertently harming clients.
questions.core_concept: In quality improvement, a performance gap relative to a benchmark is a signal to investigate, not immediately act. Root-cause analysis—a structured method for identifying contributing factors before selecting interventions—is the evidence-based first step in any improvement cycle (PDSA, Lean, Six Sigma) and is required by occupational therapy professional standards for data-driven, ethical practice.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the performance gap like a warning light on a car dashboard. The right response is not to put tape over the light (change the measure), press the accelerator harder (increase intensity blindly), or argue the gauge is wrong (more frequent readings). The right response is to open the hood and diagnose before you fix anything. Root-cause analysis is that diagnostic step—it ensures the solution matches the real problem.
questions.topic: Quality Improvement — Outcome Measurement and Root-Cause Analysis in Inpatient Rehabilitation

options.label: A
options.text: Immediately revise all current client treatment plans to add a daily high-intensity upper-extremity training session to close the performance gap.
options.incorrect_rationale: Changing treatment plans before understanding why outcomes lag the benchmark is premature and potentially unsafe; the cause of the gap may be unrelated to treatment intensity (e.g., case mix or discharge timing).

options.label: B
options.text: Recommend replacing the FIM with a different standardized measure that may better reflect the unit's actual client population and yield more favorable scores.
options.incorrect_rationale: Switching outcome measures to obtain more favorable numbers is a form of measurement gaming that undermines accountability and does not address the underlying cause of poor performance.

options.label: C
options.text: Conduct a root-cause analysis by examining documentation, staffing patterns, case mix, and treatment intensity to identify factors driving the gap between unit outcomes and the national benchmark.

options.label: D
options.text: Increase the frequency of FIM assessments from admission and discharge only to weekly intervals so that incremental gains are captured in the efficiency calculation.
options.incorrect_rationale: FIM efficiency is calculated from admission to discharge scores divided by length of stay, so more frequent intermediate assessments do not change the efficiency metric and do not address the performance gap.

questions.stem: The OT is consulting with Marcus's teacher to implement low-cost, inclusive sensory supports in the general education classroom. Which recommendation is MOST appropriate to introduce FIRST?
questions.correct_rationale: Marcus's most prominent classroom barriers are proprioceptive seeking (out-of-seat behavior, crashing, pencil chewing) and difficulty sustaining arousal during structured tasks. A dynamic seating cushion provides continuous low-level proprioceptive input passively during instruction, and scheduled movement breaks (heavy work) meet his sensory-seeking needs in a structured, predictable way. Both strategies are evidence-supported, minimally disruptive, target the identified SPM-2 deficits, and preserve full inclusion — key priorities in school-based OT practice.
questions.core_concept: When selecting classroom sensory supports, OTs prioritize strategies that are evidence-based, directly target the student's primary sensory processing needs identified through assessment, and maintain the least restrictive educational environment. Compensatory or exclusionary strategies are reserved for when less restrictive, participation-preserving options have been trialed and found insufficient.
questions.explain_differently: Marcus's nervous system is essentially 'hungry' for proprioceptive input all day — that is why he crashes into things and chews on his pencil. A wobble seat and movement breaks feed that hunger in a safe, structured way so he does not have to seek it disruptively. You are working with his sensory system, not around it, while keeping him fully part of the classroom.
questions.topic: OT_EXP

options.label: A
options.text: Seat Marcus at a desk isolated from his peers to minimize auditory and tactile distractions.
options.incorrect_rationale: Isolating Marcus from peers sacrifices social participation and peer inclusion — key occupational priorities for school-age children — and represents a restrictive strategy that should be reserved only after less restrictive options have been exhausted.

options.label: B
options.text: Allow Marcus to wear noise-canceling headphones during all instructional periods.
options.incorrect_rationale: Noise-canceling headphones primarily address auditory sensitivity; the SPM-2 identified proprioceptive and tactile processing as Marcus's primary areas of concern, so this does not target his most impairing deficits.

options.label: C
options.text: Replace all art curriculum materials with texture-neutral alternatives to prevent tactile aversions.
options.incorrect_rationale: Removing all art materials is excessively restrictive, limits curriculum access, does not build adaptive capacity, and fails to address Marcus's broader proprioceptive and regulatory presentation.

options.label: D
options.text: Provide Marcus with a dynamic seating option such as a wobble cushion and schedule brief movement breaks every 20 to 30 minutes.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist wants to identify the occupational performance issues that matter most to a client and establish baseline scores that can be used to measure change over time from the client's perspective. Which assessment tool is MOST appropriate for this purpose?
questions.correct_rationale: The Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM) is a semi-structured interview in which the client identifies and rates the importance of self-care, productivity, and leisure performance issues, then rates their own performance and satisfaction on a 1-10 scale. Because both baseline and follow-up ratings come from the client, the COPM directly detects client-perceived change over time and is explicitly designed for client-centered priority setting — making it the best fit for both goals stated in the stem.
questions.core_concept: Client-centered outcome measurement in OT relies on tools that capture the client's own perspective on what occupational performance problems are most important and how much those problems improve. The COPM operationalizes this by combining a priority-identification interview with client self-ratings of performance and satisfaction, enabling both goal-setting and outcome measurement within a single instrument.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the COPM as handing the "expert" role to the client: the client decides which daily activities are the biggest problems, scores how well they currently do them, and scores how satisfied they are. The therapist just facilitates. Because the client provides the numbers at the start and again after intervention, you get a before-and-after picture entirely through the client's eyes — something no clinician-rated checklist can give you.
questions.topic: Occupational Performance Assessment — Client-Centered Outcome Measures

options.label: A
options.text: Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM)
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer and has no distractor rationale.

options.label: B
options.text: Functional Independence Measure (FIM)
options.incorrect_rationale: The FIM is a clinician-rated measure of functional independence across ADL and mobility domains; it does not capture client-identified priorities or client-rated satisfaction.

options.label: C
options.text: Assessment of Motor and Process Skills (AMPS)
options.incorrect_rationale: The AMPS is an observational performance-analysis tool that measures the quality of motor and process skills during ADL tasks; it does not elicit or prioritize client-identified occupational concerns.

options.label: D
options.text: Barthel Index
options.incorrect_rationale: The Barthel Index is a standardized ADL checklist scored by the clinician or caregiver; it does not identify what the client considers most important or rate the client's own perception of performance.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man is admitted to inpatient rehabilitation 10 days after a right hemispheric CVA. He presents with left hemiplegia, left hemispatial neglect confirmed on the Catherine Bergego Scale, and impaired safety awareness. During morning ADL training, the occupational therapist observes he consistently omits the left side of his face during shaving and collides with objects on his left side. Which intervention approach has the strongest evidence for improving his functional ADL performance related to the neglect?
questions.correct_rationale: Visual scanning training — teaching the patient to deliberately anchor gaze at the left boundary of the workspace and systematically sweep rightward before and during each step — is the most evidence-supported occupational therapy intervention for reducing the functional impact of hemispatial neglect in ADLs. It directly compensates for the perceptual deficit by substituting a voluntary, learned strategy for the automatic attentional orienting that is impaired, and multiple RCTs and systematic reviews (including Cochrane-level evidence) demonstrate its efficacy for improving ADL performance and reducing neglect-related errors.
questions.core_concept: Hemispatial neglect is a perceptual-attentional deficit — not a motor deficit — and therefore requires perceptual or cognitive compensatory strategies rather than motor facilitation approaches. Visual scanning training is the occupational therapy intervention with the strongest evidence base for translating neglect remediation into functional ADL gains because it directly retrains the voluntary attentional system to compensate for impaired automatic spatial orienting.
questions.explain_differently: Imagine the brain's attention system as a spotlight that should automatically sweep across the full visual field. After a right CVA, that spotlight gets stuck pointing right and never reaches the left side — the patient is not choosing to ignore the left, the spotlight is broken. Motor treatments like NDT and CIMT tune the spotlight's motor controls, but they do not fix where it points. Scanning training is like installing a manual override: the patient learns to physically grab the spotlight with a deliberate head turn and verbal anchor ("find the left edge first") every single time, so the broken automatic system is bypassed by a trained conscious one. That override applies directly during shaving, dressing, and eating — which is why it produces functional ADL gains.
questions.topic: Hemispatial Neglect — Assessment and Evidence-Based Intervention in Stroke Rehabilitation

options.label: A
options.text: Neurodevelopmental treatment (NDT) focused on facilitating weight-bearing and sensory input through the left upper extremity during tabletop tasks
options.incorrect_rationale: NDT targets motor control and postural facilitation; it does not address the perceptual-attentional deficit of hemispatial neglect and lacks evidence for improving neglect symptoms or neglect-related ADL errors.

options.label: B
options.text: Visual scanning training with systematic verbal cueing to anchor at the left boundary and sweep right during each ADL task

options.label: C
options.text: Mirror therapy directed at the neglected left side during structured tabletop activities to improve visual attention
options.incorrect_rationale: Mirror therapy is primarily indicated for motor recovery and phantom limb pain through cortical reorganization; it is not a validated intervention for hemispatial neglect and does not substitute for attentional scanning strategies.

options.label: D
options.text: Constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT) to promote increased active use of the left arm during dressing and grooming
options.incorrect_rationale: CIMT addresses motor recovery in the affected limb and requires meaningful residual voluntary movement; it does not target the perceptual-attentional mechanism underlying hemispatial neglect and is contraindicated with severe hemiplegia.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes the concept of cultural safety in occupational therapy practice?
questions.correct_rationale: Cultural safety is an outcome defined by the recipient of care, not by the provider. It requires that clients feel their cultural identity, values, and worldview are genuinely respected AND that the inherent power differential between clinician and client — shaped by systemic, historical, and social factors — is explicitly recognized and addressed. Option B captures both the client-defined nature of the concept and the necessary acknowledgment of power dynamics, which are the defining features that distinguish cultural safety from cultural competence or cultural sensitivity.
questions.core_concept: Cultural safety (originating from Maori nursing scholarship and adopted across health professions) is distinct from cultural competence: it is an outcome determined by the client, not a skill set held by the clinician. It requires the practitioner to reflect on and address structural power imbalances — including those rooted in colonialism and systemic racism — and to center the client's own sense of safety and respect within the therapeutic relationship.
questions.explain_differently: Think of cultural safety like asking "Did the passenger feel safe on the flight?" rather than "Does the pilot know aviation rules?" A therapist can memorize cultural facts (competence) but if the client still walks away feeling dismissed, judged, or powerless, cultural safety has not been achieved. Safety is the client's verdict, not the therapist's report card — and it requires actively naming and leveling the power gap that exists whenever a professional holds authority over a client's care.
questions.topic: Cultural Safety in Occupational Therapy Practice

options.label: A
options.text: The occupational therapist demonstrates knowledge of the cultural practices and traditions of every client group they serve.
options.incorrect_rationale: This describes cultural knowledge or cultural competence, not cultural safety; cultural safety is defined by the client's experience, not the therapist's information base.

options.label: B
options.text: The therapy environment is decorated with culturally relevant artwork and materials representing the populations served by the clinic.
options.incorrect_rationale: Environmental decoration may contribute to a welcoming atmosphere but does not constitute cultural safety, which is an experiential and relational concept centered on the client.

options.label: C
options.text: The client experiences the therapeutic encounter as one in which their cultural identity is respected and power imbalances within the relationship are acknowledged.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer.

options.label: D
options.text: The occupational therapist completes annual mandatory cultural competency training modules as part of continuing professional development.
options.incorrect_rationale: Completing training is a professional development activity; it does not in itself produce or guarantee that any individual client experiences cultural safety in practice.

questions.stem: An experienced occupational therapist volunteers to meet monthly with a new graduate OT to discuss complex cases, reflect on professional identity, and set career goals. This ongoing relationship BEST exemplifies which form of engagement in the profession?
questions.correct_rationale: Mentorship is a voluntary, ongoing professional relationship in which a more experienced OT intentionally supports a less experienced colleague's professional growth, identity formation, and career trajectory. The scenario describes exactly this: a peer-initiated, goal-directed relationship focused on professional development rather than formal oversight of client care or structured coursework.
questions.core_concept: Mentorship is a distinct form of professional engagement in occupational therapy in which a seasoned practitioner guides a newer colleague's career development, professional reasoning, and professional identity — separate from clinical supervision (which carries accountability for client outcomes), continuing education (structured learning for competency maintenance), and fieldwork education (student training prior to licensure).
questions.explain_differently: Think of mentorship like a GPS for a road trip you are taking for the first time: the mentor has already driven that route and helps you navigate decisions, avoid pitfalls, and reach your destination — but they are not in the driver's seat responsible for your passengers (that is supervision), and they are not a classroom teaching you to drive (that is continuing education). The mentor's sole job is to help YOU grow as a professional over time.
questions.topic: Mentorship and Engagement in the Profession

options.label: A
options.text: Clinical supervision
options.incorrect_rationale: Clinical supervision involves formal, accountable oversight of clinical work and client outcomes — often required for licensure — not the career-guidance relationship described.

options.label: B
options.text: Continuing education
options.incorrect_rationale: Continuing education refers to structured learning activities (courses, workshops, CEUs) completed to maintain or expand clinical competence, not an interpersonal guidance relationship.

options.label: C
options.text: Fieldwork education
options.incorrect_rationale: Fieldwork education is supervised clinical training provided to OT students prior to entry-level practice, not to licensed new graduate clinicians.

options.label: D
options.text: Mentorship
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer; no incorrect rationale applies.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist in an urban acute care hospital is working with a 68-year-old First Nations woman who had a stroke four weeks ago. The woman communicates primarily through her adult daughter because her English is limited. The interprofessional team recommends transfer to a long-term care facility, citing documented safety risks with home discharge. Through her daughter, the client has consistently expressed a strong desire to return to her remote reserve community, where extended family are prepared to provide care. The OT conducts a telephone home assessment and identifies structural access barriers and limited on-reserve rehabilitation services. Which action BEST reflects culturally safe, client-centred, and anti-oppressive occupational therapy practice?
questions.correct_rationale: Option B operationalises three intersecting OT obligations simultaneously. First, advocacy: rather than accepting structural barriers as fixed, the OT works to dismantle them by drawing on Indigenous health liaison services and community networks — a direct anti-oppressive move. Second, cultural safety: involving a cultural broker ensures the client's goals are understood within her cultural context, and prevents the daughter from inadvertently filtering or re-interpreting her mother's wishes. Third, client-centredness: the plan is built with the client and community, not for them. None of the other options achieve all three without either overriding autonomy (A), pathologising disagreement (C), or creating harmful delay (D).
questions.core_concept: Cultural safety in OT requires the practitioner to actively examine and address how institutional power, systemic racism, and structural barriers shape the clinical encounter — it is not achieved merely by respecting stated preferences, but by dismantling the conditions that constrain those preferences. Anti-oppressive, client-centred practice demands that the OT advocate across system levels while ensuring the client's authentic voice (not a proxy's interpretation of it) drives the plan.
questions.explain_differently: Think of this as the difference between a locked door and an open hallway. The team sees a locked door (structural barriers, limited rehab) and says "you can't go home." An OT practising cultural safety asks: who has the key, and can we find it together? Option B sends the OT to look for the key — community supports, liaison services, a cultural broker who can genuinely hear the client — instead of accepting the door as permanently locked or questioning whether the client even knows what she wants. The other options either accept the locked door (A), question the client's right to choose (C), or stand motionless searching for a perfect key that may never arrive (D).
questions.topic: CEJ_JUSTICE — Anti-Oppressive Practice, Cultural Safety, and Indigenous Client-Centred Discharge Planning

options.label: A
options.text: Advocate for the client's return to her community by engaging Indigenous health liaison services, co-creating a discharge plan with the family and community supports, and — with the aid of a cultural broker or interpreter — confirming the client's own goals directly rather than relying solely on her daughter's account.

options.label: B
options.text: Document the client's preference, then align with the team's recommendation for long-term care, because the structural barriers and limited rehabilitation access on the reserve create an unacceptable safety risk that overrides the client's wishes.
options.incorrect_rationale: Deferring to the team recommendation without advocacy treats safety concerns as absolute barriers rather than challenges to problem-solve, reproduces institutional bias, and fails to centre client autonomy — a core feature of anti-oppressive practice.

options.label: C
options.text: Initiate a formal cognitive capacity assessment to determine whether the client can make this decision independently before proceeding with discharge planning in either direction.
options.incorrect_rationale: No clinical evidence of cognitive impairment is presented; defaulting to a capacity assessment when a client disagrees with the medical team reflects a paternalistic 'capacity-as-compliance' stance that is oppressive, particularly toward Indigenous clients already subject to systemic distrust of medical institutions.

options.label: D
options.text: Pause discharge planning until a fully qualified interpreter fluent in the client's Indigenous language can be secured for all future team discussions, to ensure nothing is miscommunicated before a decision is made.
options.incorrect_rationale: While addressing language barriers is essential, indefinitely halting planning while awaiting a perfect language match prolongs unnecessary hospitalization and is not feasible in most acute settings; the OT should mobilize available Indigenous liaison and interpreter supports rather than waiting for ideal conditions.

questions.stem: Marcus's classroom teacher asks the OT for a single, first-line strategy to help Marcus sustain attention and remain on task during a 20-minute written assignment. Given his proprioceptive low registration pattern, which recommendation is MOST appropriate?
questions.correct_rationale: Low proprioceptive registration means Marcus's nervous system requires greater-than-typical proprioceptive input to achieve and maintain an alert, organized state for participation. A weighted lap pad delivers sustained deep-pressure proprioceptive input and can increase arousal and body awareness without disrupting the classroom. A structured movement break at the midpoint provides additional proprioceptive input through joint compression and muscle activity, resetting Marcus's arousal level to sustain the second half of the task. These strategies directly target the neurological pattern identified on the Sensory Profile 2 and are low-cost, non-stigmatizing, and classroom-compatible.
questions.core_concept: Sensory processing patterns identified through standardized tools should directly inform classroom strategy selection. Low proprioceptive registration is addressed by increasing the intensity or frequency of proprioceptive inputs (deep pressure, heavy work, structured movement) to support self-regulation and sustained occupational engagement.
questions.explain_differently: Think of proprioceptive low registration like a radio with a very weak signal — the brain is not picking up enough of the body's position and movement information to stay alert and organized. A weighted lap pad boosts that signal at the antenna, giving the nervous system the extra proprioceptive input it needs to tune in and stay focused. The movement break is like hitting the reception tower at the midpoint to keep the signal strong for the rest of the assignment.
questions.topic: OT_EXP

options.label: A
options.text: Allow Marcus to complete all written work using voice-to-text software on a tablet to eliminate the handwriting demand entirely
